A local team that takes pride in building things right. Serving Everett and Snohomish County with quality craftsmanship and honest pricing.
Built on Quality, Trust, and Hard Work
NW General Contractor is the trade name of NW Style Homes 1 LLC, a Washington-registered general contractor (NWSTYSH768DA) based in Everett.

NW General Contractor was founded with a simple idea: homeowners in Snohomish County deserve a contractor they can actually trust. Someone who shows up when they say they will, communicates honestly about costs and timelines, and delivers work they are genuinely proud of.

We are a full-service general contracting company based in Everett, Washington. We handle everything from kitchen and bathroom remodeling to roofing, siding, foundation repair, and complete home renovations. Whether you need a single room updated or your entire home transformed, we manage the project from start to finish so you do not have to.

NW General Contractor started from a real passion for building and a frustration with how the industry often treats homeowners. Too many people in the Everett area have been burned by contractors who overpromise and underdeliver — missed deadlines, surprise costs, poor communication, or work that does not hold up.

We set out to do things differently. Every project begins with a detailed, written estimate. We keep you informed throughout the process, return your calls and messages promptly, and stand behind our work long after the last nail is driven. Our reputation is built one project at a time, and we take that seriously.

As a small, hands-on team, we bring the kind of personal attention that larger companies cannot match. You will not be passed between sales reps and project managers who have never picked up a hammer. The people you meet during your estimate are the same people who will be building your project.
We are a full-service general contractor, which means we handle a wide range of residential construction and remodeling projects:
— Kitchens, bathrooms, flooring, painting, and whole-home renovations. We handle the design coordination, demolition, rough-in, and finish work.
— Roofing, siding, windows, doors, and foundation repair. We protect your home from the Pacific Northwest weather with quality materials and expert installation.
— Decks, patios, pergolas, fencing, outdoor kitchens, and concrete work. We help you make the most of your property year-round.
— Home additions, ADU construction, and detached garages. We manage the full build from permitting through final inspection.
— Built-in shelving, custom trim, wainscoting, mantels, and specialty woodwork that adds character and function to your home.
— Detailed written estimates with itemized costs. No hidden fees, no surprise change orders. If something changes mid-project, we discuss it with you before any additional work happens.

— We source materials from trusted suppliers and choose products rated for Pacific Northwest conditions. From moisture-resistant framing to UV-stable exterior finishes, every selection is made with longevity in mind.

— You will have a dedicated point of contact throughout your project. Regular updates, responsive to calls and texts, and honest about timelines. If something comes up, you will hear about it from us before you have to ask.
— Fully licensed with Washington State, carrying general liability insurance and a surety bond. Your home and your investment are protected.
— We respect your home. Daily cleanup, protective coverings on floors and fixtures, and careful attention to your landscaping and property throughout the project.

We are proud to serve homeowners across Snohomish County, including Everett, Marysville, Lake Stevens, Lynnwood, Mukilteo, Snohomish, Mill Creek, Bothell, and Arlington. As a local company, we understand the unique character of each community — from the historic craftsman homes of downtown Everett to the newer developments in Lake Stevens and the waterfront properties along Mukilteo.

Snohomish County is one of the fastest-growing regions in Washington state, and much of the existing housing stock is 30 to 50 years old or more. Whether you are updating an aging kitchen, replacing a worn-out roof, converting a garage into an ADU, or completely renovating a mid-century home, we have the experience to handle the surprises that come with opening up walls and working on established homes.

We would love to hear about your project. Whether you are in the early planning stages or ready to break ground, contact us for a free, no-obligation estimate. We will visit your home, listen to your ideas, and provide a detailed quote so you know exactly what to expect.
Get a free, no-obligation estimate for your next project. We serve all of Snohomish County.

text_segments: Dependable home remodeling for Arlington's rural properties and growing neighborhoods. Farmhouse renovations, room additions, and modern updates.
Home Remodeling for Arlington's Changing Landscape

Arlington sits at the northern gateway of Snohomish County, a community of approximately 20,000 residents that embodies the transition between the suburban development of the county's southern half and the agricultural and forested landscape that stretches north toward Skagit County and the North Cascades. The Stillaguamish River winds through the valley floor below town, dairy farms still operate on the surrounding flats, and the Cascade foothills rise to the east. Yet Arlington is also a community in transformation, with new subdivisions, expanding retail, and a growing population that has discovered the appeal of small-town living within commuting distance of Everett and the greater Seattle area. NW General Contractor serves Arlington homeowners across this full spectrum, from century-old farmhouses to brand-new construction.

along the Stillaguamish River bottom is Arlington's agricultural heartland, where properties measured in acres rather than square feet define the landscape. The farmhouses that dot the valley range from turn-of-the-century wood-frame structures to mid-century homes built during the region's dairy farming heyday. These properties present renovation challenges that suburban contractors may not be equipped to handle: foundations that have settled unevenly over decades on the valley's alluvial soils, outdated septic systems that must be considered during any expansion, well water systems that affect plumbing decisions, and structures that have been added onto informally over generations without always following building codes.

services for Stilly Valley farmhouses address these practical realities head-on. We begin with thorough structural assessments, leveling floors, reinforcing foundations, and bringing electrical and plumbing up to current code before focusing on the cosmetic transformation.

in these farmhouses often involves creating the large, open kitchen that has become the modern farmhouse ideal: a central island with seating, open shelving mixed with cabinetry, apron-front sinks, and a layout that connects the kitchen to informal dining and living areas where families actually spend their time.

neighborhood and the streets surrounding downtown Arlington contain the city's most established residential areas. Homes here were built from the 1920s through the 1960s, ranging from modest bungalows and Cape Cod cottages to larger colonial and ranch-style homes on tree-lined streets. This is classic small-town Washington, with sidewalks, mature elms, and the kind of neighborhood character that attracts buyers looking for something more authentic than a cookie-cutter subdivision.
Remodeling in Haller Park and downtown Arlington focuses on modernizing these well-located homes while respecting their neighborhood context.

is a common starting point, as many of these homes have only one full bathroom, often with original fixtures, worn tile, and inadequate ventilation. We reconfigure small bathrooms to maximize space, add en-suite bathrooms where possible, and install modern fixtures that improve daily comfort. For homes with only one bathroom, adding a second bathroom through a
or by converting underutilized space can be a practical investment that significantly improves livability and resale value.

commercial area along Interstate 5, though technically part of the Marysville and unincorporated Snohomish County area, serves as the primary retail hub for Arlington residents. The residential neighborhoods east and north of Smokey Point, within Arlington's city limits and urban growth boundary, represent the city's newest suburban development. These neighborhoods feature homes built from the 2000s through today, with contemporary floor plans, attached garages, and the amenities that new construction provides.

While these newer homes do not need the comprehensive renovation that older properties require, Arlington's newer homeowners frequently request upgrades that personalize builder-standard homes. Popular projects include
that creates outdoor entertaining space on the relatively compact lots of newer subdivisions,
that adds built-in mudrooms, pantry shelving, and garage organization systems, and kitchen upgrades that replace builder-grade countertops and fixtures with premium materials.

Outside Arlington's city limits, the surrounding rural areas are home to properties on five, ten, or twenty-plus acre parcels. These include working hobby farms, horse properties, and homesteads where families have chosen a more self-sufficient lifestyle. Renovation needs on these properties are often substantial and varied. Older barns may be converted into workshops or living space. Detached structures may need to be brought up to code. Kitchens in older ranch houses may need complete overhauls to serve families who grow and preserve their own food.

on rural Arlington properties offers unique opportunities. County zoning regulations for properties outside city limits may differ from municipal rules, and the larger lot sizes can accommodate more substantial detached living units. We build ADUs on Arlington-area acreages for a variety of purposes: housing for farmworkers or caretakers, independent living spaces for aging parents, and rental units that generate supplemental income for property owners.

Arlington residents enjoy a lifestyle that revolves around the outdoors. The Centennial Trail passes through town, the Stillaguamish River offers fishing and recreation, and the surrounding foothills provide endless hiking opportunities. This outdoor orientation drives demand for covered porches, screened-in patios, and generous decks that serve as three-season living spaces. We design and build outdoor structures that reflect Arlington's rural character, using natural wood, timber-frame construction, and stone elements that complement the surrounding landscape rather than fighting it.

Projects within Arlington city limits go through the City of Arlington's Community Development department, while properties in unincorporated areas fall under Snohomish County's jurisdiction. The two processes differ in timelines, fees, and specific requirements. NW General Contractor is experienced with both jurisdictions and ensures that every Arlington-area project is properly permitted and inspected. We handle all paperwork so homeowners can focus on the exciting decisions about their home's transformation. Call us at

text_segments: Expert home remodeling for Bothell's diverse neighborhoods. From tech-worker kitchens to historic Main Street renovations, we do it all.
Remodeling Bothell: Where Tech Meets Tradition

Bothell occupies a unique position in the Puget Sound region, straddling the King County and Snohomish County line with a combined population of approximately 50,000 residents. The city has undergone a remarkable renaissance over the past two decades, driven by the growth of the University of Washington Bothell campus, the expansion of the Canyon Park technology corridor, and a revitalized downtown that has transformed from a sleepy Main Street into a vibrant dining and entertainment destination. This evolution has attracted a diverse population of tech professionals, university faculty, young families, and longtime residents, all of whom are investing in their homes. NW General Contractor serves the Snohomish County side of Bothell with remodeling expertise that matches the city's sophisticated and varied housing market.

area in north Bothell has become one of the Eastside's most important technology and business corridors. Companies in software, biotech, and engineering have established offices here, and the surrounding residential neighborhoods have attracted their employees. Homes in Canyon Park were largely built in the 1980s through 2000s, ranging from townhomes and condominiums to single-family homes on wooded lots. These are homeowners with high expectations and the budgets to match them.

projects in Canyon Park frequently involve premium specifications: integrated Sub-Zero and Wolf appliance packages, custom cabinetry with full-extension drawers and specialized storage solutions, waterfall quartz islands with flush-mounted cooktops, and designer lighting schemes with layered task, ambient, and accent fixtures. These are kitchens designed for homeowners who entertain frequently and appreciate culinary excellence. Our team works with top material suppliers and maintains the precision installation skills that premium finishes demand.

area southeast of Canyon Park features a mix of residential styles, from established neighborhoods with homes built in the 1970s and 1980s to newer developments that have filled in previously undeveloped parcels. North Creek's proximity to the Burke-Gilman Trail and North Creek Park makes it popular with active families who value outdoor recreation and community green spaces.
Older North Creek homes are prime candidates for

. These properties, typically ramblers and split-levels with three to four bedrooms, have solid bones but dated everything else. We help North Creek homeowners plan comprehensive renovations that modernize kitchens and bathrooms, open up floor plans, upgrade windows and insulation for energy efficiency, and add the kind of design details that make a house feel custom. Our approach is to create a phased renovation plan that allows homeowners to live in their home during construction when possible, minimizing disruption while maximizing results.

shopping area and the neighborhoods along Bothell's historic Main Street represent the city's original character. Homes in this area include Craftsman bungalows from the early 1900s, midcentury ramblers, and postwar capes that reflect Bothell's evolution from a small lumber town to a suburban community. The city's investment in Main Street revitalization, including streetscape improvements, new restaurants, and the Pop Keeney Stadium area, has made these central neighborhoods increasingly desirable.
Renovation in historic Bothell requires balancing modern expectations with existing character. Our

work in older Bothell homes addresses common challenges: small original bathrooms that need reconfiguration, aging cast-iron plumbing that should be replaced, and inadequate ventilation that leads to moisture problems. We design bathrooms that feel spacious and current while complementing the home's age and style, using tile patterns, fixtures, and vanities that bridge traditional and contemporary aesthetics.

The University of Washington Bothell campus, located along the Sammamish River on the city's southern edge, has profoundly influenced the local housing market. Faculty, staff, and graduate students seek housing in nearby neighborhoods, and the university's continued growth has supported strong property values. Homeowners near the campus frequently invest in

, building accessory dwelling units that serve as rental properties for university-affiliated tenants or as home offices for remote workers. Bothell's ADU regulations are among the most accommodating in the region, and we have extensive experience navigating the permitting process for both attached and detached units.
Outdoor Living for Bothell's Wooded Lots
Many Bothell properties sit on wooded lots that provide privacy and a natural setting that feels worlds away from the urban core.

on these properties takes advantage of the natural surroundings, with multi-level deck designs that work with the terrain rather than against it. We build decks using composite materials that resist the moisture-rich Pacific Northwest environment, incorporate screening and roof structures for rain protection, and design outdoor spaces that extend the home's living area into the trees. Hot tub installations, outdoor fireplaces, and screened porches are popular additions that make Bothell's outdoor spaces usable throughout the year.
Home Additions for Growing Bothell Families

Bothell's excellent school district and family-oriented neighborhoods attract growing families who quickly outgrow their starter homes. Rather than selling and moving, many choose to add space through
. We build master suite additions, family room expansions, and second-story additions that give families the room they need while keeping them in the community they love. Our

work adds the finishing touches: window seats in children's bedrooms, mudroom cubbies for a family of five, and home library built-ins for the remote worker who needs a dedicated, well-designed workspace.

Because Bothell spans two counties, the permitting process depends on which side of the county line your property falls on. Properties in the Snohomish County portion of Bothell work with the Snohomish County Planning and Development Services department, while those in King County follow a different process. text_segments: Your hometown remodeling experts serving all Everett neighborhoods. Licensed, bonded, and insured for residential construction.

As the largest city in Snohomish County with a population of over 110,000 residents, Everett is a city defined by its rich industrial history, stunning waterfront, and remarkably diverse housing stock. NW General Contractor is proud to call Everett home, and we bring decades of local construction expertise to every project we undertake in the city. From the historic craftsman bungalows of Port Gardner to the modern developments near Silver Lake, we understand the unique characteristics and challenges of Everett homes at every age and price point.
Everett's neighborhoods each carry a distinct character that influences remodeling priorities. In the

neighborhoods near the waterfront, you will find many of the city's oldest homes, some dating back to the early 1900s. These craftsman-style and Victorian-era residences often feature original woodwork, built-in cabinetry, and layouts that reflect a different era of living. Homeowners here frequently seek kitchen remodels that honor the home's historic charm while introducing modern amenities, along with bathroom renovations that replace aging plumbing and fixtures.

neighborhoods, situated along the Snohomish River, feature a mix of mid-century ranches and split-levels built during Everett's postwar boom. These homes typically have smaller kitchens, single bathrooms, and dated electrical systems. We regularly help Delta and Riverside homeowners with

Everett's housing history creates predictable remodeling patterns. A significant portion of the city's housing stock was built before 1978, which means lead paint and asbestos are common concerns during renovation. Our team is trained in safe abatement practices and works with certified testing laboratories to ensure every project meets current safety standards.

The Boeing Everett Factory and Naval Station Everett bring a steady flow of workers and military families to the area, many of whom purchase older homes and invest in updates. We frequently work with these homeowners on projects ranging from straightforward
to full-scale renovations that transform dated properties into modern, comfortable homes.
With the City of Everett actively encouraging accessory dwelling units to address the region's housing shortage,

Whether you are building a detached backyard cottage or converting a garage into a rental unit, we handle every phase from design and permitting through final inspection. Everett's ADU regulations allow units up to 800 square feet on most single-family lots, and we have completed numerous ADU projects across the city.

Everett's Community Development Department oversees building permits for residential construction. As a licensed contractor with deep experience navigating Everett's permitting process, we manage all permit applications, plan reviews, and inspections on behalf of our clients. Projects in the Port Gardner Historic District may require additional design review to ensure renovations complement the neighborhood's architectural heritage. We are well-versed in these requirements and can guide homeowners through the approval process efficiently.

text_segments: General Contractor in Lake Stevens, WA
Deck building, home remodeling, and outdoor living specialists for Lake Stevens lakefront and residential properties.
Building and Remodeling for Lake Stevens Living

Lake Stevens holds the distinction of being the fastest-growing city in Snohomish County, with a population that has nearly doubled in recent years to over 39,000 residents. The city's namesake lake, the largest in the county at over 1,000 acres, sits at the heart of a community that values outdoor recreation, family life, and the kind of natural beauty that draws people away from the urban core. NW General Contractor serves Lake Stevens homeowners with remodeling and construction services designed for the way people actually live here, where the backyard deck matters as much as the kitchen, and where lakefront properties demand a contractor who understands waterfront construction.

Lake Stevens' most distinctive homes are the properties that line the shores of the lake itself. These range from modest cottages built in the 1940s and 1950s as summer getaways to substantial year-round homes constructed more recently. Lakefront remodeling presents unique challenges that require specialized experience. Shoreline setback regulations, critical areas ordinances, and the need to manage stormwater on sloped lots all demand a contractor who has navigated these requirements before.

projects in Lake Stevens, constructing multi-level decks that step down sloped lots to create outdoor entertaining spaces with water views. Composite decking materials are particularly popular here, as they resist the moisture that is inherent to lakeside living and require far less maintenance than traditional wood. Our lakefront deck designs incorporate built-in seating, cable railing systems that preserve sight lines, and integrated lighting for evening use.
Lake Stevens Neighborhoods and Home Styles
Beyond the lakefront, Lake Stevens has grown outward through a series of residential developments, each with its own character. The
area east of the lake features a mix of established homes from the 1980s and 1990s alongside newer subdivisions. Hartford homeowners often seek
projects that open up compartmentalized floor plans, remove walls between kitchen and dining areas, and create the open-concept living spaces that modern families prefer.

area, situated on the hillside north of town, offers some of Lake Stevens' most sought-after views. Homes here tend to be larger and newer, built from the late 1990s through the 2010s. Soper Hill homeowners frequently invest in

that transforms standard master bathrooms into spa-like retreats, with walk-in showers, heated floors, and freestanding soaking tubs. The emphasis in this area is on luxury upgrades that match the quality of the views.

and the downtown core include some of Lake Stevens' older housing stock, with modest ramblers and split-levels from the 1960s and 1970s. These homes are attractive to first-time buyers and families priced out of closer-in communities, and they often need significant updates. Our
services help these homeowners modernize aging systems, update dated interiors, and add square footage where original floor plans fall short.
Outdoor Living: The Heart of Lake Stevens Life

If there is one thing that defines Lake Stevens homeowners, it is their commitment to outdoor living. The lake, the trails, the views of the Cascades, and the long summer evenings all point toward a lifestyle that extends well beyond the front door. This is why outdoor living space construction is one of our most requested services in Lake Stevens. Beyond decks, we build covered patios, outdoor kitchens, pergolas, and screened porches that allow homeowners to enjoy the outdoors through the Pacific Northwest's varied weather. We also construct fire pit areas and built-in seating that make backyards functional gathering spaces three seasons out of the year.
With property values rising and lot sizes generally larger than what you find closer to Seattle, Lake Stevens is an excellent market for

Others build ADUs for aging parents who want to live close to family while maintaining their independence. Lake Stevens' zoning codes support ADU construction on most single-family lots, and our team manages the complete process from design and permitting through construction and final inspection.

The construction of new schools, the expansion of retail along the Highway 9 and 204 corridors, and the steady arrival of new residents all signal that Lake Stevens' growth trajectory will continue. text_segments: Historic home renovation and thoughtful remodeling for the Antique Capital of the Northwest. Preserving character while modernizing comfort.
Preserving History, Building for Today in Snohomish

The City of Snohomish holds a special place in Snohomish County, not just as the county seat's namesake, but as a community that has consciously preserved its heritage while the region around it has rapidly developed. Known as the "Antique Capital of the Northwest," Snohomish's charming downtown along First Street is lined with Victorian-era commercial buildings housing antique shops, restaurants, and small businesses. The residential neighborhoods surrounding downtown contain some of the finest examples of late 19th and early 20th century architecture in the Pacific Northwest. NW General Contractor brings specialized expertise in historic renovation and thoughtful remodeling to this unique community of approximately 10,000 residents.

The residential streets adjacent to Snohomish's historic downtown are defined by homes built between 1880 and 1920. Queen Anne Victorians with their ornate gingerbread trim, Craftsman bungalows with deep front porches and exposed rafter tails, and Colonial Revival homes with symmetrical facades line avenues shaded by mature trees. These homes represent an irreplaceable architectural legacy, and renovating them demands a contractor who understands the difference between restoring a home and simply updating it.

in Snohomish's historic core prioritizes preservation of character-defining features. Original woodwork, pocket doors, built-in china cabinets, hardwood floors, and decorative plaster details are carefully protected during renovation. Where historic elements have deteriorated, we restore rather than replace, using period-appropriate techniques and materials. At the same time, we modernize the systems that make these homes livable: upgrading knob-and-tube wiring to modern electrical, replacing galvanized plumbing with copper or PEX, adding proper insulation without compromising wall profiles, and installing efficient heating systems that work within the constraints of historic construction.
Kitchen Renovation in Historic Snohomish Homes

in Snohomish's older homes presents a distinctive design challenge. The original kitchens in Victorian and Craftsman homes were utilitarian spaces, often small and separate from the rest of the house. Today's homeowners want kitchens that function as the heart of the home, open to dining and living areas, with modern appliances and generous counter space. Achieving this in a historic home requires structural sensitivity, as opening up walls may involve rerouting structural loads, and the kitchen design needs to complement rather than clash with the home's period character.

We design Snohomish kitchen remodels that bridge historical and contemporary aesthetics. Inset cabinetry with period-appropriate hardware, apron-front sinks, and furniture-style islands can create a modern kitchen that looks and feels right in a home built over a century ago. We match trim profiles, respect ceiling heights, and select materials that honor the craftsmanship of the original construction while delivering every modern convenience.
The Pilchuck Area and Rural Properties

area east of town transitions into the rural landscape that still defines much of Snohomish's character. Properties here include farmhouses from the early to mid-1900s, ranch-style homes from the 1960s and 1970s, and newer construction on larger acreages. Farmhouse kitchens may need complete overhauls, including structural reinforcement of floors that have settled over decades.
on rural properties can be more expansive, taking advantage of larger lots and fewer setback constraints.

on Pilchuck properties, where homeowners want covered outdoor living spaces that take advantage of pastoral views and the quiet rural setting. Wrap-around porches, screened sleeping porches, and timber-frame pergolas complement the farmhouse aesthetic that homeowners in this area cherish.

, Snohomish's small municipal airport, include a mix of residential styles from various decades. This area attracts aviation enthusiasts and families who appreciate the area's unique character. projects in this area often involve expanding original bathrooms that were built to minimal dimensions, adding walk-in showers, double vanities, and proper ventilation that older homes lack.

skills are most fully realized. This level of craftsmanship requires woodworking skills, historical knowledge, and a genuine respect for the homes we work in. is gaining interest. Homeowners on larger lots are exploring detached ADUs designed to complement the architectural style of their primary residence. text_segments: ADU Regulations in Snohomish County: What Homeowners Need to Know (2026)
A complete guide to building an accessory dwelling unit in Snohomish County, WA
Published February 2026 | By NW General Contractor

Accessory dwelling units (ADUs) have become one of the hottest topics in Snohomish County real estate and construction. Thanks to sweeping changes in Washington state law and updated local regulations, building an ADU on your property is now easier, more affordable, and more practical than ever before.

Whether you're looking to generate rental income, create a space for aging parents, or simply increase your property value, this guide covers everything you need to know about ADU regulations in Snohomish County as of 2026.
is a secondary housing unit on a single-family residential lot. It has its own kitchen, bathroom, and sleeping area, making it a fully independent living space. ADUs come in three main types:

A standalone structure separate from the primary home, often built in the backyard. This is the most common type of new ADU construction in Snohomish County. DADUs can be purpose-built as a small cottage or built above a detached garage. They offer the most privacy for both the homeowner and the tenant.

An addition or conversion that is physically connected to the primary house. This could be a basement apartment, an above-garage unit, or a bump-out addition with a separate entrance. Attached ADUs are typically less expensive than detached units because they share walls, foundation, or roof structure with the main home.

Converting an existing attached or detached garage into a living space. Garage conversions are popular because the basic structure already exists, reducing construction costs. However, they require significant work to meet residential building codes including insulation, plumbing, egress windows, and ventilation.
Washington HB 1337: The Law That Changed Everything

, one of the most progressive ADU laws in the country. This law went into effect in phases through 2023 and 2024, and it fundamentally changed what local jurisdictions can and cannot regulate regarding ADUs.
Homeowners can now build up to two ADUs on a single-family lot — one attached and one detached. Previously, most jurisdictions only allowed one.

The state eliminated the requirement that the property owner must live on-site. You can now rent both the primary home and the ADU(s). This was a game-changer for investors and homeowners who want to move but keep the property.
Local jurisdictions can no longer require extra off-street parking spaces for ADUs. This removed one of the biggest practical barriers to ADU construction, especially on smaller lots.
Impact fees for ADUs are capped at 50% of the fees charged for the primary dwelling, making the permitting process less expensive.
Cities and counties must process ADU permit applications within the same timeframe as other residential permits.
Jurisdictions cannot impose design requirements on ADUs that are more restrictive than those applied to the primary dwelling.

In March 2025, Snohomish County updated its local ADU regulations to fully comply with HB 1337 and further streamline the process. These updated regulations apply to unincorporated Snohomish County. Cities within the county (Everett, Marysville, Lake Stevens, etc.) have their own codes, though all must comply with state law.
ADUs are now permitted in virtually all residential zones throughout unincorporated Snohomish County
Lot coverage and setback requirements have been relaxed for ADU construction
The county created an expedited review process for ADU applications that use pre-approved state building plans
Connection fees for water and sewer have been adjusted to be more proportional to the ADU's size
Height limits for detached ADUs have been increased to allow two-story structures in many zones
Under current state and county law, ADUs are allowed in
where single-family homes are permitted. This includes:
Single-family residential zones (R-5, R-7, R-9, R-12, etc.)

The main limitations relate to lot-specific constraints like critical areas (wetlands, steep slopes, flood zones), septic system capacity for rural properties, and utility availability. If your property is on a septic system rather than municipal sewer, you'll need to verify the system can handle the additional load.
Size limits vary slightly depending on whether you're in an incorporated city or unincorporated Snohomish County:
Up to 1,000 square feet or 50% of the primary dwelling's floor area, whichever is less
Up to 1,000 square feet in most jurisdictions. Some cities within the county allow up to 1,200 square feet
Detached ADUs can generally be up to 24 feet tall in urban areas, allowing for a two-story structure or a unit above a garage
Typically 5 feet from side and rear property lines for detached ADUs, though this varies by jurisdiction
A 1,000-square-foot ADU is roughly equivalent to a generous one-bedroom or a compact two-bedroom apartment — plenty of space for a single person, couple, or small family.

as a requirement for ADUs. Local jurisdictions cannot require additional off-street parking spaces specifically for an ADU. This is significant because on many Snohomish County lots, finding space for an additional parking spot was a major obstacle.

You may still need to maintain the existing parking requirement for your primary dwelling (typically two off-street spaces). If you're converting a garage to an ADU, you should verify with your local jurisdiction whether you need to provide replacement parking for the lost garage spaces.
Here's what the ADU permitting process looks like in Snohomish County:
Meet with the planning department to discuss your project, site constraints, and requirements. This can save significant time and money by identifying issues early. 1-2 weeks.
Work with a designer or architect to create construction plans. Using pre-approved state plans can save time here. 2-6 weeks depending on complexity.
File your application with the relevant jurisdiction along with plans, site plans, and fees. The City of Everett, for example, has an online portal for permit applications.
The jurisdiction reviews your plans for code compliance. Expect 4-8 weeks for standard review, or 2-4 weeks for pre-approved plans.
Address any comments or required changes. 1-3 weeks.
Once approved, you receive your building permit and can begin construction.
Foundation, framing, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and final inspections are required at various stages.
After final inspection, you receive authorization to occupy the ADU.
Total timeline from application to occupancy:
6-14 months is typical for a detached ADU, depending on the complexity of the project and construction schedule.
ADU construction costs in Snohomish County vary significantly based on the type and finishes:
Internal Conversion (Basement or Space Within Home)

Converting existing finished or unfinished space within the home. Costs depend on whether plumbing and egress already exist. A basement conversion typically requires waterproofing, egress windows, a kitchenette, bathroom, and separate entrance.

Converting an existing garage into a living space. Requires insulation, drywall, flooring, plumbing (kitchen and bath), electrical upgrades, HVAC, egress windows, and finishing work. The structure already exists, which saves on foundation and framing costs.

Building a new standalone structure from the ground up. This is the most expensive option but offers the most flexibility in design and the highest potential rental income. Costs include site preparation, foundation, framing, roofing, siding, interior finishes, utilities, and landscaping. Premium finishes, difficult site conditions (slope, trees, access), or larger units push costs toward the higher end.
$5,000-$15,000 depending on jurisdiction and project scope
$5,000-$20,000 for water, sewer, and electrical connections
$3,000-$15,000 for grading, drainage, and access paths
$5,000-$15,000 for custom plans (or significantly less with pre-approved plans)
$2,000-$8,000 to restore the yard after construction
Washington state has developed a library of
to reduce costs and speed up permitting. These plans have already been reviewed for state building code compliance, which means local jurisdictions can expedite their review process.
Faster permit approval (often weeks instead of months)
Lower design costs (no need for custom architecture)
Proven designs that meet all code requirements
Multiple floor plans and styles available

Pre-approved plans are a great starting point, though some homeowners prefer custom designs that better suit their property and aesthetic preferences. Your contractor can advise on which approach makes the most sense for your situation.
One of the primary motivations for building an ADU is rental income. In Snohomish County, current rental rates for ADU-sized units are strong:
These rates mean a well-built ADU can generate
. For a $300,000 detached ADU, that represents a 6-9% gross return before expenses — a strong return for a real estate investment that also increases your property value.

Short-term rental (Airbnb, VRBO) rates are higher but come with more management overhead and may be subject to local short-term rental regulations. Check with your jurisdiction before planning to use an ADU as a short-term rental.
ADUs generally increase property value in the Snohomish County market. While the exact amount varies, a well-built ADU typically adds
to the property's appraised value. A $300,000 ADU might add $180,000-$240,000 in property value.

The combination of increased property value and rental income makes ADUs one of the strongest real estate investments available to homeowners in the current market. With the elimination of owner-occupancy requirements, ADU properties have also become attractive to real estate investors.
Can I build an ADU on my property in Snohomish County?

Most likely yes. Under Washington HB 1337 and updated Snohomish County regulations effective March 2025, ADUs are now allowed in virtually all residential zones. You can build up to two ADUs on a single-family lot — one attached (AADU) and one detached (DADU). Check with your local jurisdiction for any remaining lot-specific requirements such as critical area restrictions or septic capacity.
How much does it cost to build an ADU in Snohomish County?

Costs vary by type. A garage conversion typically runs $180,000-$220,000. A detached ADU (new construction) ranges from $250,000-$450,000 depending on size, finishes, and site conditions. An internal conversion of existing space runs $80,000-$150,000. Permit fees and utility connections add $10,000-$35,000 to any of these options.
Do I need to live on the property to have an ADU in Snohomish County?

No. Washington HB 1337 eliminated owner-occupancy requirements statewide. You are not required to live on the property to rent out an ADU. This means you can rent both the primary residence and the ADU, which has opened up ADU construction as a viable investment strategy.
How big can an ADU be in Snohomish County?

Under current regulations, attached ADUs (AADUs) can be up to 1,000 square feet or 50% of the primary dwelling's floor area, whichever is less. Detached ADUs (DADUs) can be up to 1,000 square feet. Some jurisdictions within Snohomish County may allow larger units — check with your local planning department for specific allowances.
How long does it take to get an ADU permit in Snohomish County?

The permit process typically takes 6-12 weeks from application to approval. Using Washington state pre-approved building plans can shorten review time significantly. Total construction time for a detached ADU is usually 4-8 months after permits are issued, making the total timeline from planning to occupancy roughly 6-14 months.
Do I need extra parking for an ADU?

In most cases, no. HB 1337 prohibits local jurisdictions from requiring additional off-street parking for ADUs. This was one of the biggest barriers to ADU construction that the state law removed. You still need to maintain existing parking requirements for your primary dwelling.

Building an ADU is a significant investment, but the regulatory landscape has never been more favorable. At NW General Contractor, we specialize in ADU construction throughout Snohomish County. How Much Does a Bathroom Remodel Cost in Everett, WA? (2026)
Published February 2026 by NW General Contractor
Bathroom Remodel Cost Overview in Everett

Bathroom remodeling in the Everett area typically costs between $6,000 and $35,000, depending on the scope of work, materials chosen, and the size of your bathroom. Snohomish County labor rates and material costs factor into these numbers. Here's a detailed breakdown to help you plan your budget.
A budget remodel focuses on cosmetic updates that refresh the look without moving plumbing or changing the layout. This includes:
This level works well for rental properties, quick refreshes before selling, or bathrooms that are structurally sound but visually dated.
A mid-range remodel is the most popular option among Everett homeowners. It typically includes:
New tile flooring and shower surround ($2,000-$5,000)
Custom vanity with quartz or granite countertop ($1,500-$3,500)
Tub-to-shower conversion or new shower enclosure ($2,500-$6,000)
New lighting plan with recessed and vanity lights ($500-$1,200)
According to Remodeling Magazine's Cost vs. Value report, a mid-range bathroom remodel recoups approximately 70.1% of its cost at resale — making it one of the best ROI projects you can do.
A high-end remodel transforms your bathroom into a spa-like retreat:
Custom tile work with designer patterns ($4,000-$8,000)
Walk-in shower with frameless glass, rain showerhead, body jets ($5,000-$10,000)
Smart features: heated toilet seat, motion-sensor faucets ($500-$2,000)
Always add a 10-20% contingency for unexpected issues — especially in older Everett homes where hidden water damage or outdated plumbing can be discovered during demolition.
Factors That Affect Cost in the Everett Area
Pre-1978 homes may need lead paint remediation. Homes built in the 1970s-1990s (common in Everett) often have galvanized pipes that should be replaced.
Snohomish County requires permits for plumbing and electrical changes. Budget $200-$500 for permit fees.
Moving plumbing or walls increases cost significantly (add $3,000-$8,000).
Porcelain tile vs. natural stone can swing costs by $2,000-$5,000.
ADA-compliant features (grab bars, curbless shower, wider doorway) add $1,000-$3,000 but increase accessibility and resale value.
Timeline: How Long Does a Bathroom Remodel Take?

Timeline can extend if permits are required, custom materials need to be ordered, or if unexpected issues are found during demolition. The best approach is to have your contractor provide a detailed timeline before work begins.
Tips to Save on Your Bathroom Remodel
— Moving plumbing is the single biggest cost driver. Keeping fixtures in the same locations saves thousands.
— Bathtub refinishing costs $300-$600 vs. $1,500-$4,000 for replacement.
— Modern porcelain tile mimics marble and slate at a fraction of the cost.
— Sometimes new fixtures, paint, and a new vanity are enough to transform the space.
— Always get at least 3 written estimates from licensed contractors.
How much does a small bathroom remodel cost in Everett?

A small bathroom remodel in Everett typically costs $6,000-$15,000, depending on the scope. Cosmetic updates run $6,000-$10,000 while more comprehensive renovations with new tile and fixtures run $10,000-$15,000.
Do I need a permit for a bathroom remodel in Snohomish County?

Yes, if you're changing plumbing or electrical systems. Cosmetic updates (paint, fixtures, vanity swaps) generally don't require permits. Check with the Snohomish County Planning & Development Services office.
How long does a bathroom remodel take?
A typical mid-range bathroom remodel in the Everett area takes 2-4 weeks. Budget remodels can be done in 1-2 weeks, while high-end projects may take 4-6 weeks.
What's the ROI on a bathroom remodel?

According to Remodeling Magazine, a mid-range bathroom remodel recoups approximately 70.1% of its cost at resale. In Snohomish County's competitive housing market, updated bathrooms are a strong selling point.
Should I remodel my bathroom before selling my home?
Often yes. Updated bathrooms are one of the top features buyers look for. Even a budget refresh ($6,000-$10,000) can make your home more competitive and potentially increase your sale price.

Decks & Patios Cost in Everett, WA (2026 Guide)
Published July 2026 by NW General Contractor

For homeowners researching decks & patios cost Everett, a practical 2026 planning range is typically $8,000–$50,000, depending on whether the project is a simple patio, new deck, major rebuild, or covered outdoor space. Materials, site access, structural work, finishes, permits, and labor can move an Everett estimate below or above that range.
What a decks & patios costs in Everett

The average cost of a decks & patios in Everett is difficult to reduce to one number because decks and patios are built differently. A deck is an elevated structure that may require footings, framing, stairs, railings, and structural connections. A patio is usually constructed at or near grade using concrete, pavers, gravel, or another hardscape material. Those differences affect labor, materials, permits, and timeline.

For early budgeting, an uncomplicated ground-level patio may typically fall around $8,000–$20,000, while a straightforward new deck may typically cost around $15,000–$40,000. Larger decks, elevated structures, premium decking, extensive stairs, covered areas, or combined deck-and-patio projects may commonly reach approximately $40,000–$100,000, depending on scope. These are planning ranges rather than quotes; site conditions and design decisions can change the actual proposal substantially.

Homeowners comparing decks & patios price per square foot Everett figures should use them cautiously. A basic patio may sometimes budget around $20–$50 per square foot, while a conventionally framed deck may often budget around $45–$100 per square foot. Complex or premium deck construction may fall around $80–$175 per square foot. Small projects can have a higher unit price because mobilization, demolition, permitting, equipment, and finish work are spread across less area.

Everett properties also vary in grade, drainage, access, and existing construction. A flat backyard with direct equipment access is usually easier to price than a sloped or confined site. Before choosing a budget from an online calculator, have the contractor identify what the price includes: demolition, disposal, excavation, footings, framing, surface materials, railings, stairs, drainage work, permits, finishes, and cleanup.

Project scope has the greatest overall influence on cost. Resurfacing a sound deck is a different project from replacing deteriorated framing, and an uncovered patio is different from a roofed outdoor living area. Size matters, but structural height, shape, stairs, guardrails, integrated seating, privacy screens, lighting preparation, and transitions to doors or walkways can matter just as much.

Labor increases when crews must remove old construction, hand-carry materials through narrow side yards, work on a slope, build high above grade, or make careful connections to an existing house. Hidden deterioration can also expand the scope after demolition. A responsible estimate should state how concealed damage will be documented, priced, and approved if it is discovered.

Materials create another large range. Pressure-treated framing and economical surface products generally cost less than premium composite decking, specialty hardwood, metal railing systems, porcelain pavers, or elaborate masonry. Material price alone does not tell the whole story: some products require additional framing, specialized fasteners, more detailed installation, or manufacturer-specific handling.

Finishes affect both appearance and maintenance. Wood decks may need cleaning, staining, or sealing, while concrete patios may include color, texture, scoring, or protective treatment. Paver patios need a properly prepared base and edge restraint. The least expensive finish at installation may not be the least expensive choice over the outdoor space's service life.

Permits and related documentation may be needed depending on the structure, location, height, attachments, electrical work, and other project details. Permit fees and preparation can add roughly $500–$3,000 to some projects, while more involved plans or professional design services may increase that planning allowance to approximately $2,000–$8,000. The applicable requirements should be confirmed for the specific Everett property rather than assumed from a neighboring project.
Overall size, elevation, shape, and structural complexity
Decking, concrete, pavers, railings, fasteners, and finish selections
Demolition, disposal, excavation, drainage, and site preparation
Backyard access, slope, soil conditions, and material-handling distance
Stairs, built-in seating, privacy features, lighting preparation, and covered areas
Permit requirements, plans, inspections, and coordination with related trades

A repair or maintenance project may typically cost around $2,000–$10,000 when the work involves cleaning, refinishing, replacing limited deck boards, or correcting a contained problem. That range assumes the primary structure can remain. If inspection reveals widespread deterioration or unsafe framing, partial repair may no longer be the appropriate scope.

A basic patio may typically fall around $8,000–$20,000 for a modest area with relatively direct access and limited site preparation. Concrete finish choices, excavation, drainage, retaining needs, paver patterns, and difficult access can push the project toward approximately $18,000–$35,000. Outdoor kitchens, substantial covers, fire features, or extensive utility work would require separate allowances and trade-specific evaluation.

A small or straightforward deck may typically range from $15,000–$30,000. A medium deck with stairs, railings, upgraded surface materials, or more demanding framing may commonly range from $25,000–$55,000. An elevated, multilevel, premium, or covered deck may fall around $50,000–$100,000, depending on engineering needs, access, structural details, and finishes.

A combined outdoor-living project involving both a deck and patio may typically budget around $35,000–$100,000. The advantage of planning them together is that elevations, stairs, drainage, pathways, and material transitions can be coordinated. The estimate should still separate major components so homeowners can see where the budget is going and evaluate optional features.

Construction time also varies by scope. A straightforward patio may usually take about 1–3 weeks after approvals and material availability. A conventional deck may usually require about 2–6 weeks. A larger, covered, or highly detailed outdoor-living project may take approximately 6–14 weeks. Weather, inspections, demolition findings, product lead times, and scope changes can extend those ranges.
Medium deck with stairs or upgrades: typically $25,000–$55,000
Complex, elevated, premium, or covered deck: typically $50,000–$100,000
How to get an accurate estimate

An accurate estimate starts with a defined scope and an on-site review. Measure the approximate area, collect inspiration photos, identify preferred materials, and decide which features are essential. Tell the contractor whether the goal is a new installation, complete replacement, resurfacing, repair, or a coordinated deck-and-patio design. Photos help communicate style, but they cannot reveal soil, framing, drainage, or access conditions.

For an existing deck, the contractor should evaluate the visible framing, surface condition, stairs, railings, supports, and connections that can be accessed. For a patio, the review should consider grade, runoff, excavation, base preparation, nearby structures, and the route crews will use to move material. Concealed conditions should be identified as an estimate limitation rather than silently assumed.

Ask for a written proposal that distinguishes included work from allowances and exclusions. It should identify demolition, disposal, structural work, surface materials, railing, stairs, finishes, site restoration, permit responsibility, and cleanup where applicable. Product names or clearly described quality levels make competing bids easier to compare than vague phrases such as standard material.

The proposed timeline should separate planning and approvals from active construction. Depending on project complexity and agency workload, design, selections, and permitting may add roughly 2–10 weeks before construction. Material ordering may overlap with part of that period, but specialty products can have longer lead times. A realistic schedule should also allow for Everett-area weather and inspection sequencing.

NW General Contractor serves Everett and Snohomish County homeowners. To request a site-specific estimate, call (425) 286-5639 with the property location, approximate dimensions, photos, desired materials, and a short description of the intended scope. The resulting estimate should reflect the actual site rather than relying only on generalized 2026 cost ranges.
Approximate length, width, height, and number of levels
Photos of the yard, house connection, access route, and existing structure
Preferred decking, railing, concrete, paver, and finish options
Features such as stairs, covers, privacy screens, seating, or lighting preparation
Clear responsibility for permits, demolition, disposal, and site restoration
Written handling process for changes or concealed damage
Smart ways to save without cutting corners

The most reliable savings come from simplifying the design before construction begins. Rectangular layouts, standard material dimensions, direct stair runs, and fewer level changes can reduce labor and waste while still producing a useful outdoor space. Keeping a patio near grade is often less structurally demanding than creating a large elevated deck, although site drainage and access still need proper consideration.

Spend where durability and safety depend on it: preparation, drainage, footings, framing, fastening, flashing, and suitable materials. Decorative upgrades are easier to defer than structural corrections. If the budget is tight, ask the contractor to separate core construction from optional items such as elaborate patterns, premium railings, built-in seating, privacy features, or a future cover.

Compare lifecycle needs as well as installation price. A lower-cost wood surface may fit the initial budget but can involve recurring cleaning and refinishing. A higher-priced composite option may reduce some maintenance, but product lines and installation requirements vary. Request at least two material packages priced for the same layout so the comparison remains meaningful.

Planning early can also limit expensive changes. Finalize dimensions, door transitions, stair locations, furniture zones, and finish selections before ordering materials. If a future hot tub, cover, outdoor kitchen, or other heavy feature is being considered, disclose it during design so the structure and utilities can be evaluated for that intended use.

Finally, keep a contingency rather than using the entire budget on visible finishes. For renovation work, a contingency of roughly 10%–20% of the estimated project range may be prudent, depending on how much existing construction is concealed. That allowance is not automatically spent; it provides room if demolition reveals deterioration, drainage problems, or other conditions that could not be confirmed beforehand.
Use a simple footprint and standard material dimensions
Price comparable basic and upgraded material packages
Preserve sound existing components only after they are evaluated
Defer optional decorative features instead of reducing structural scope
Finalize selections before ordering and construction
Plan a roughly 10%–20% contingency, depending on uncertainty
How much does a decks & patios cost in Everett?

A deck or patio in Everett may typically cost around $8,000–$50,000, while larger, elevated, premium, covered, or combined projects may range from approximately $40,000–$100,000. The actual price depends on size, structure, materials, access, permits, and site preparation.
What has the biggest impact on decks & patios cost?

Project scope usually has the biggest impact. Size, elevation, demolition, structural framing, stairs, railings, drainage, material selections, finishes, backyard access, and permit requirements can each move a project within or beyond the typical planning ranges.
How long does a decks & patios usually take?

A straightforward patio may usually take about 1–3 weeks of construction, while a conventional deck may take roughly 2–6 weeks. Larger or covered projects may require approximately 6–14 weeks, with design, permitting, inspections, weather, and material lead times potentially adding about 2–10 weeks.
Do I need a permit for a decks & patios?

A permit may be required depending on the project's structure, height, location, attachment to the house, and related electrical or other work. Requirements can differ by property and scope, so they should be confirmed with the appropriate authority before construction begins.
How do I get an accurate decks & patios estimate?

Schedule an on-site review and provide approximate dimensions, photos, preferred materials, and a clear feature list. A kitchen remodel in the Everett area typically takes 4-8 weeks from demolition to completion, depending on scope. Here's what affects the timeline and what to expect week by week.
1-2 weeks — New paint, hardware, fixtures, and minor updates
4-6 weeks — New cabinets, countertops, flooring, appliances, same layout
6-8 weeks — Layout changes, structural work, full renovation
8-12+ weeks — Everything new, possibly moving walls, plumbing, electrical
Final design decisions and material selections
Materials ordered (cabinets often take 2-4 weeks to arrive)
Existing cabinets, countertops, and flooring removed
Countertops templated and installed (often 1 week between template and install)
Custom cabinets and special-order materials can take 4-8 weeks. Order early.
Snohomish County permits can take 2-4 weeks for review.
Water damage, mold, outdated wiring, or plumbing issues discovered during demo.
Changing your mind mid-project is the #1 cause of delays. Finalize decisions before construction starts.
If exterior work is involved (windows, doors), PNW rain can cause delays.
Tips to Keep Your Remodel on Schedule
Make all design decisions before demolition
— Finalize cabinets, countertops, tile, fixtures, and appliances before day 1.
— Especially cabinets, which can take 2-6 weeks. Have everything on-site before construction starts.
— A microwave, coffee maker, and mini-fridge in another room will get you through.
— Weekly check-ins keep everyone aligned and catch issues early.
— 10-20% buffer handles unexpected discoveries without derailing the project.
Can I live in my house during a kitchen remodel?

Yes, most homeowners stay in their home during a kitchen remodel. Set up a temporary kitchen with a microwave, mini-fridge, and coffee maker in another room. The inconvenience typically lasts 4-6 weeks.
What's the fastest a kitchen can be remodeled?
A cosmetic refresh (paint, hardware, fixtures) can be done in 1-2 weeks. A full mid-range remodel with new cabinets and countertops typically takes a minimum of 4 weeks.
Do I need a permit for a kitchen remodel in Snohomish County?
If you're changing the layout, moving plumbing, or doing electrical work, yes. Cosmetic updates generally don't require permits. Your contractor should handle the permit process.
When is the best time to remodel a kitchen in the Pacific Northwest?

Late spring through early fall offers the best conditions, but kitchen remodels are interior work and can be done year-round. Winter is often a good time because contractors may have more availability.

text_segments: How to Choose a General Contractor in Everett, WA (2026 Guide)
Everything you need to know to hire a trustworthy contractor for your home improvement project
Published February 2026 | By NW General Contractor

Hiring a general contractor is one of the most important decisions you'll make during any home improvement project. The right contractor delivers quality work on time and on budget. The wrong one can cost you thousands in delays, poor workmanship, and stress. In the Everett area, where home values continue to climb and the construction market is competitive, knowing how to vet a contractor properly is essential.
This guide walks you through every step of the process, from verifying licenses to spotting red flags, so you can make a confident decision.
This is the single most important step, and it takes about 30 seconds.
Every general contractor in Washington state must be registered with the Department of Labor & Industries (L&I).
Operating without registration is illegal, and hiring an unregistered contractor strips you of most legal protections if something goes wrong.
Enter the contractor's business name or UBI (Unified Business Identifier) number
Review their registration status, specialty, and any infractions
The L&I lookup will show you:
Whether the registration is active and current
The contractor's specialty (general, electrical, plumbing, etc.)
Any complaints, violations, or infractions on file
If a contractor can't provide a registration number or doesn't appear in the L&I database, stop the conversation there. No exceptions.
2. Confirm the $30,000 Surety Bond and Liability Insurance
Washington state requires all registered contractors to carry a
. This bond protects you, the homeowner, if the contractor:
Fails to complete the work as agreed
Doesn't pay subcontractors or material suppliers (who could then lien your property)
In addition to the bond, a reputable contractor should carry
for their employees. Ask for a Certificate of Insurance (COI) and verify it's current. If a contractor's worker is injured on your property and they don't have workers' comp, you could be liable.
Both the bond and insurance status are verifiable through the L&I website. If anything has lapsed, that's a red flag.
Online reviews provide insight into a contractor's reliability, quality of work, communication style, and how they handle problems. Check multiple platforms for a well-rounded picture:

The most widely used review platform. Look at both the overall rating and read individual reviews, especially recent ones. Pay attention to how the contractor responds to negative reviews — professionalism matters.
Tends to have more detailed reviews. Filter for "Contractors" in the Everett area.
Check for the contractor's BBB rating and any filed complaints. An "A+" rating with zero complaints is ideal, but also look at how complaints were resolved.
Community recommendations from your actual neighbors carry significant weight.
What to look for in reviews:
Consistency of positive feedback across platforms
Specific mentions of completed projects similar to yours
How the contractor handled unexpected issues or change orders
Whether projects were completed on time and on budget
Be cautious of contractors with no online presence at all. In 2026, a legitimate, established contractor should have reviews.

Getting multiple estimates isn't just about finding the lowest price — it's about understanding the range of approaches and costs for your project. Three estimates is the minimum; the more complex your project, the more valuable additional perspectives become.
What a Good Estimate Should Include
Specific descriptions of what will be done, not vague summaries
Brands, models, quantities, and quality levels for all major materials
Broken out separately from materials where possible
Start date, milestones, and expected completion date
When payments are due and what triggers each payment
What's covered and for how long
How additional work or changes will be priced and approved
If an estimate is just a single number on a piece of paper, that's not a real estimate — it's a guess. Detailed estimates protect both you and the contractor by setting clear expectations.
Be wary of the lowest bid.

If one estimate is significantly lower than the others (25%+ below the average), there's usually a reason: they're cutting corners on materials, underestimating the scope, using unlicensed subcontractors, or planning to hit you with change orders later.
5. Ask for References and Recent Project Photos
Any contractor worth hiring should be proud to share their work. Ask for:
(within the last 12 months). Actually call them. Ask about the quality of work, communication, timeline accuracy, and whether they'd hire the contractor again.
similar to what you're planning. A kitchen remodeler should be able to show you finished kitchens. An ADU builder should have ADU photos.
An active project you can visit
(with the homeowner's permission). Seeing a jobsite in progress tells you a lot about how a contractor operates — cleanliness, organization, crew professionalism, and quality of in-progress work.
Was the project completed on time and on budget?
How did the contractor handle unexpected issues?
Was communication consistent throughout the project?
Were there any surprises with the final cost?
Would you hire this contractor again?
A solid contract protects everyone. Before signing, make sure the contract clearly addresses these elements:
Everything that will be done, described in detail. If it's not in the contract, don't assume it's included.
Start date, completion date, and consequences for significant delays (excluding weather and material delays beyond the contractor's control).

Tied to milestones, not arbitrary dates. A typical schedule might be 10% deposit, 30% at demolition completion, 30% at rough-in completion, and 30% at final completion. Never pay more than 10-15% upfront.
How changes to the scope will be documented, priced, and approved. Every change should be in writing before work begins.
Exact products, not "or equivalent." If specific materials are important to you, they need to be in the contract.

What the contractor warrants, for how long, and how warranty claims are handled. Washington state provides a 6-year statute of repose for construction defects, but contractor warranties often cover workmanship for 1-2 years.
How disagreements will be handled (mediation, arbitration, etc.).
Who pulls the permits and pays for them. This should be the contractor.

Take the time to read the contract thoroughly. Ask questions about anything you don't understand. A good contractor welcomes questions about their contract — they want you to feel comfortable and informed.
After years in the industry, these are the warning signs that should make you walk away:
Illegal in Washington state. Full stop.
Legitimate contractors accept checks and often credit cards. Cash-only requests are a tax evasion signal and leave you with no payment trail.
A handshake deal offers you zero legal protection.
No legitimate contractor asks for more than 10-15% as a deposit. Demanding full payment before work begins is a classic scam.
"This price is only good today" is a high-pressure sales tactic. A fair estimate should be valid for at least 30 days.
A P.O. Box only or no address at all makes it difficult to pursue the contractor if problems arise.
Every established contractor has satisfied customers. If they won't share references, there's a reason.
A legitimate contractor can produce a Certificate of Insurance within 24 hours.
Storm chasers who show up uninvited after weather events are notorious for poor work and insurance fraud.
An estimate that's 30-40% below others is likely missing something or setting you up for change orders.
8. Questions to Ask During the Estimate Visit
When a contractor comes to your home for an estimate, use the visit to evaluate both their expertise and professionalism. Good questions to ask:
How long have you been in business, and how long have you worked in the Everett/Snohomish County area?
Who will be the day-to-day project manager on my job?
Do you use your own crew or subcontractors? Are the subcontractors also licensed and insured?
How do you handle communication and updates during the project?
What's your approach to keeping the worksite clean and respecting my home?
Have you done projects similar to mine? Can you show me examples?
How do you handle issues that come up mid-project?
What's your current workload and when could you start?
What warranties do you offer on your work?

Pay attention to how the contractor conducts the estimate visit. Do they arrive on time? Do they take measurements and notes? Do they ask you questions about your goals and preferences? A contractor who's thorough during the estimate is likely to be thorough during the project.
When choosing a contractor in Everett, there are real advantages to working with a local company:

Everett, Snohomish County, and other local jurisdictions each have their own permitting processes and code interpretations. A local contractor knows these systems and has working relationships with building departments.
Local contractors have vetted teams of plumbers, electricians, and other specialists who know the area and deliver consistent quality.
A local contractor lives and works in your community. Their reputation is their livelihood. They can't just move on to the next city if a project goes sideways.
Local contractors know the best suppliers in the area and can often get better pricing and faster delivery on materials.
If something needs attention after the project is complete, a local contractor can respond quickly. A contractor based two hours away is far less likely to make a timely warranty visit.
When you hire local, your money stays in the local economy. You're supporting your neighbors and community.
How do I verify a contractor's license in Washington state?
Visit the Washington Department of Labor & Industries contractor verification page at

. Enter the contractor's name or license number to check their registration status, bond information, insurance coverage, and any complaints or violations on file. This free lookup takes about 30 seconds and should be the first thing you do.
How many estimates should I get for a home remodel?

We recommend getting at least three written estimates from different licensed contractors. This gives you a range of pricing, allows you to compare approaches, and helps you identify outliers — both suspiciously high and suspiciously low. Make sure each contractor is bidding on the same scope of work for an accurate comparison.
What are red flags when hiring a contractor?

Major red flags include: no state contractor registration, requesting cash-only payment, no written contract, demanding full payment upfront, pressure to sign immediately, no physical business address, unwillingness to provide references, and being unable to show proof of insurance. Any of these should be a dealbreaker — even if the price is attractive.
What should a contractor's estimate include?

A detailed estimate should include: a complete scope of work with specific descriptions, material specifications and quantities, labor costs, permit fees, a project timeline with milestones, payment schedule tied to completed work, warranty information, and a clear change order process. Vague estimates with a single lump-sum number are a warning sign.
Do contractors in Washington need a bond?

Yes. Washington state requires all registered contractors to carry a $30,000 surety bond. This bond protects homeowners if the contractor fails to complete the work, doesn't pay subcontractors, or causes property damage. You can verify a contractor's bond status through the L&I website at lni.wa.gov/verify.
