How Much Does a Kitchen Remodel Cost in Everett, WA? (2026)
A detailed guide to kitchen renovation pricing in the Everett and Snohomish County area
Published February 2026 | By NW General Contractor
If you're planning a kitchen remodel in Everett, Washington, one of the first questions on your mind is probably:
how much is this going to cost?
It's a fair question, and the answer depends on the scope of work, the materials you choose, and the current state of your kitchen.
In 2026, kitchen remodel costs in the Everett area range from around
$10,000 for a basic refresh to $60,000 or more for a full custom renovation
. The Puget Sound region tends to run slightly higher than national averages due to strong demand for skilled labor, higher material transport costs, and local permitting requirements.

We've put together this comprehensive guide based on our experience remodeling kitchens across Snohomish County. Whether you're updating a starter home in North Everett or renovating a larger property in Silver Lake, here's what you can realistically expect to spend.

A budget kitchen remodel focuses on making the most impactful visual changes without moving plumbing, electrical, or walls. This level of renovation works well for homeowners who want to modernize an outdated kitchen without a massive investment, or for those preparing a home for sale.
What You Get at This Price Point
Instead of replacing cabinets entirely, you refinish or paint existing cabinet boxes and install new doors and hardware. This alone can transform the look of a kitchen for $3,000-$6,000.
Modern laminate countertops have come a long way and can mimic the look of stone for a fraction of the cost. Expect to pay $1,500-$3,000 for new countertops at this level.
Luxury vinyl plank (LVP) is the go-to choice for budget remodels. It's waterproof, durable, and looks great. Budget $1,200-$2,500 for materials and installation.
New faucet, cabinet pulls, and light fixtures can make a surprising difference. Plan for $500-$1,500.
A subway tile backsplash and fresh paint on the walls round out the refresh. $800-$2,000.
If your current appliances are functional but dated, this budget may allow for one or two new mid-range appliances.

A budget remodel keeps the existing kitchen layout intact. You're working with the current footprint, which means no permits needed for most of the work (unless you're changing electrical or plumbing connections).

This is the sweet spot for most Everett homeowners. A mid-range remodel gives you the best balance of quality, aesthetics, and return on investment. You're getting real upgrades that will last 15-20 years and significantly improve your daily experience in the kitchen.
Full replacement of cabinets with semi-custom options from brands like KraftMaid or Diamond. Soft-close hinges, pull-out drawers, and better storage solutions. $8,000-$14,000.
Quartz has become the most popular countertop choice in our area. It's durable, low-maintenance, and available in hundreds of colors and patterns. $3,500-$6,000 installed.
Porcelain tile or engineered hardwood that matches the rest of the home. $2,500-$4,500.
A matching stainless steel suite including range, refrigerator, dishwasher, and microwave from a brand like Samsung, LG, or KitchenAid. $3,000-$6,000.
New under-cabinet lighting, additional outlets, and possibly relocating a sink or dishwasher. $2,000-$4,000.
A designer tile backsplash adds personality and protects walls. $1,000-$2,500.
Removing a small non-load-bearing wall or adding an island is possible at this budget. Structural changes add cost but can dramatically improve flow.

At the mid-range level, you'll likely need permits from the City of Everett for plumbing and electrical work. Your contractor should handle the permitting process, which typically adds 2-4 weeks to the project timeline.

A high-end kitchen remodel is a full transformation. Everything is selected for quality, durability, and design. This level of renovation is common in neighborhoods like Mukilteo, Mill Creek, and the nicer areas of South Everett where home values support the investment.
Built to your exact specifications with premium materials like maple, cherry, or walnut. Features include integrated organizers, glass-front doors, and custom finishes. $15,000-$25,000.
High-end quartz, natural marble, quartzite, or even concrete countertops with waterfall edges. $5,000-$10,000.
Brands like Sub-Zero, Wolf, Thermador, or Miele. A professional range alone can run $4,000-$10,000. Full suite: $8,000-$18,000.
Hand-laid mosaic backsplashes, heated tile floors, and designer patterns. $3,000-$6,000.
Moving walls, relocating plumbing and gas lines, adding windows, or opening up to an adjacent room. Structural engineering may be required. $5,000-$12,000.
Layered lighting plan with recessed fixtures, pendant lights, under-cabinet LEDs, and dimmer controls. $2,000-$4,000.
Built-in wine storage, pot filler faucet, integrated charging stations, touchless faucets, and custom range hoods.
Regardless of your total budget, the percentage breakdown tends to stay fairly consistent. Understanding where your money goes helps you make smarter allocation decisions:
Cabinets consistently take the biggest chunk. If you're looking to cut costs without sacrificing the overall feel, refacing or painting existing cabinets is the single most effective move.
Factors That Affect Cost in the Everett Area
Kitchen remodel costs aren't the same everywhere. Several factors specific to Everett and Snohomish County affect what you'll pay:

Skilled trades in the Puget Sound region command higher wages than the national average. The Seattle metro area's construction boom over the past decade has kept demand for qualified tradespeople high. Expect labor rates of $50-$85 per hour for experienced installers, plumbers, and electricians in the Everett area.
Building permits in the City of Everett are based on the project's value. For a kitchen remodel, expect to pay
depending on the scope of work. Unincorporated Snohomish County has its own fee schedule. Permit review times typically run 2-4 weeks, so factor that into your project timeline.

While the Pacific Northwest has good access to building materials, specialty items like imported tile or custom cabinetry may have longer lead times. Local suppliers like Lowe's, Home Depot, and specialty showrooms in Everett and Lynnwood stock most standard materials, but custom orders can take 4-8 weeks.

Everett has a mix of older craftsman homes (built 1900-1940s) and newer construction. Older homes often have surprises behind the walls: outdated wiring, galvanized plumbing, or inadequate support structures. Budget an extra 10-15% contingency if your home was built before 1970.

The construction season in the Pacific Northwest peaks from April through October. Scheduling your remodel during the slower winter months (November-March) may get you better availability and occasionally better pricing from contractors.
A kitchen remodel is one of the best investments you can make in your home. According to the
, a major kitchen remodel in the Pacific region recoups approximately
at resale. Minor kitchen remodels perform even better, often recouping 85% or more.

Beyond resale value, a remodeled kitchen improves your daily quality of life and can make your home easier to sell when the time comes. In the competitive Snohomish County real estate market, an updated kitchen is often the deciding factor for buyers.
Tips to Save Money Without Sacrificing Quality
After years of remodeling kitchens across Everett and Snohomish County, here are our top recommendations for getting the most value from your budget:
Moving plumbing and gas lines is expensive. If your current layout works reasonably well, invest in better materials instead of relocating fixtures.
If your cabinet boxes are structurally sound, painting or refacing them saves $5,000-$10,000 compared to full replacement.
Quartz countertops are more durable, require zero maintenance, and cost less than premium granite or marble.
Skip the appliance upgrades if yours are recent:
If your appliances are less than 5-7 years old and working well, put that money into cabinets or countertops instead.
Removing old cabinets, flooring, or backsplash yourself can save $500-$1,500 in labor. Just don't touch plumbing, electrical, or structural elements.
Major holidays (Memorial Day, Labor Day, Black Friday) bring significant appliance discounts. Plan ahead and buy during sales.
A good GC manages subcontractors, materials, and scheduling. Their markup is offset by trade discounts on materials and avoiding costly mistakes.
Understanding the timeline helps you plan for disruption. Here's what to expect at each level:
3-5 weeks from start to finish. Minimal disruption.
6-10 weeks including permit processing. Plan to be without a functional kitchen for 3-6 weeks.
10-16 weeks or more. Custom materials have longer lead times, and structural work adds complexity. Plan for 6-10 weeks without a kitchen.
In all cases, add 2-4 weeks at the front end for design, material selection, and permit processing through the City of Everett or Snohomish County.
How much does a kitchen remodel cost in Everett, WA?

Kitchen remodel costs in Everett range from $10,000 to $60,000 or more. A budget remodel runs $10,000-$22,000, a mid-range renovation costs $22,000-$40,000, and a high-end custom remodel starts at $40,000 and can exceed $60,000. The final cost depends on materials, scope of work, and whether you're changing the kitchen layout.
What is the ROI of a kitchen remodel in Washington state?

According to the Cost vs. Value Report, a major kitchen remodel in the Pacific Northwest recoups approximately 77.6% of the investment at resale. Minor kitchen remodels can recoup even more, sometimes exceeding 85%. In the competitive Snohomish County housing market, an updated kitchen can also help your home sell faster.
How long does a kitchen remodel take in Everett?

A budget kitchen remodel typically takes 3-5 weeks, a mid-range remodel takes 6-10 weeks, and a high-end kitchen renovation can take 10-16 weeks or more. Permit processing in Snohomish County adds 2-4 weeks to the overall timeline. Custom material orders can add additional lead time.
Do I need a permit for a kitchen remodel in Everett?

It depends on the scope of work. Cosmetic updates like painting, replacing countertops, and installing new flooring generally don't require permits. However, any work involving plumbing changes, electrical modifications, structural alterations, or moving walls requires permits from the City of Everett. A licensed general contractor should handle the permitting process for you.
What is the most expensive part of a kitchen remodel?

Cabinets are typically the most expensive component, accounting for 30-35% of the total budget. For a $30,000 mid-range remodel, that means $9,000-$10,500 goes to cabinetry alone. Labor and installation is the second highest cost at 20-25%, followed by appliances at 15-20%.

Do I Need a Permit for My Remodel in Snohomish County? (2026 Guide)
Published February 2026 by NW General Contractor
When You Need a Permit in Snohomish County
In Snohomish County, building permits are required for work that changes the structure, plumbing, electrical, or mechanical systems of your home. Here's a clear breakdown.
Adding or relocating plumbing (new sink, shower, toilet)
Electrical panel upgrades or new circuits
Deck construction (over 200 sq ft or 30+ inches above grade)
Window or door size changes (altering the opening)
Converting a garage to living space
Work That Generally Does NOT Need a Permit
Replacing fixtures in the same location (faucet, light fixture, toilet)
Replacing appliances (same location, same fuel type)
2-4 weeks for standard projects, 4-8 weeks for complex projects
Permits are obtained through Snohomish County Planning & Development Services or your city's building department (Everett, Marysville, etc. have their own departments).
Inspections ensure work meets building codes and is safe for your family
Unpermitted work may not be covered by your homeowner's insurance
Unpermitted work must be disclosed and can reduce your home's value or kill a sale
Working without required permits can result in fines of $500-$5,000+, plus the cost of tearing out and redoing work
If unpermitted work causes injury or damage, you face serious legal exposure
A licensed contractor will handle the permit process for you as part of the project.
How much does a building permit cost in Snohomish County?
Residential building permits in Snohomish County typically cost $200-$2,000+ depending on the project value. Plumbing and electrical permits are additional at $100-$300 each.
How long does it take to get a permit in Snohomish County?
Standard residential permits typically take 2-4 weeks for review. Complex projects may take 4-8 weeks.
What happens if I remodel without a permit?
You can face fines of $500-$5,000+, be required to tear out completed work, and have difficulty selling your home. Unpermitted work may also void your homeowner's insurance.
A licensed general contractor should handle the entire permit process as part of your project, including applications, plan submissions, and scheduling inspections.

How Much Does a New Roof Cost in Snohomish County? (2026)
Complete pricing guide with material comparisons for homeowners in Everett, Marysville, Lake Stevens, and surrounding areas
Published April 2026 | By NW General Contractor
What Does a New Roof Actually Cost in 2026?

If you're a homeowner in Snohomish County looking at a roof replacement, you've probably seen wildly different numbers online. That's because roofing costs depend heavily on material choice, roof size and complexity, and local labor rates — and most national guides don't reflect Pacific Northwest pricing.
Here's the reality for 2026: an average roof replacement in Snohomish County costs
on a typical 2,500-square-foot home. Budget options like 3-tab shingles can come in around $16,000, while premium materials like cedar shake or tile can push well past $60,000.

The Pacific Northwest's relentless rain, moss growth, and temperature swings make material choice more critical here than almost anywhere else in the country. A roof that lasts 30 years in Arizona might only last 20 in Everett. This guide breaks down real 2026 pricing for every major roofing material, explains Snohomish County permit requirements, and helps you decide which option gives you the best return on your investment.
Roofing Cost by Material (2026 Snohomish County Pricing)
The table below shows installed costs for a typical 2,500-square-foot roof in Snohomish County, including tear-off of one existing layer, materials, labor, and disposal.

Note: These prices include tear-off, disposal, underlayment, flashing, and standard labor. Complex roofs with steep pitches, multiple valleys, or difficult access will cost more. All pricing reflects Snohomish County labor rates as of early 2026.
Asphalt vs. Metal: Which Is Better for Washington Rain?
This is the most common question we hear from Snohomish County homeowners, and the answer depends on your budget and how long you plan to stay in your home.
Good. Modern architectural shingles have excellent water-shedding capability and algae-resistant coatings
25 - 35 years with proper ventilation and regular moss treatment
Annual moss removal recommended, professional inspection every 3 - 5 years
Most manufacturers offer 30 - 50 year limited warranties
Excellent. Water slides off immediately. No granule loss, no water absorption, no moss adhesion
50 - 70+ years — many metal roofs outlast the home itself
Virtually none. Occasional debris clearing and fastener inspection
40 - 50 year paint warranties, lifetime structural warranties from top manufacturers

If you're staying in your home for 15+ years, metal roofing's long-term ROI often wins in the Pacific Northwest. You'll avoid one or two full asphalt replacements over the same period, and you'll spend almost nothing on maintenance. But if budget is tight or you're planning to sell within 10 years, architectural asphalt shingles deliver excellent performance at a fraction of the cost. Both are solid choices — there's no wrong answer here.
Cedar Shake: The Classic PNW Choice

There's nothing quite like a cedar shake roof on a Pacific Northwest home. The warm, natural look blends perfectly with the evergreen landscape, and it's a material with deep roots in the region's building tradition. Cedar shake remains a popular choice in upscale neighborhoods throughout Snohomish County, particularly in Mukilteo, Mill Creek, and the rural areas around Snohomish and Lake Stevens.
But beauty comes with responsibility. Here's what to know before choosing cedar:

Washington state building codes require cedar shakes to be fire-retardant treated. Class B or Class C fire ratings are the minimum, and some jurisdictions within Snohomish County may have additional requirements, especially in wildland-urban interface zones near Arlington and eastern parts of the county.

Snohomish County's wet climate is paradise for moss and lichen. Cedar roofs need regular treatment with zinc or copper strips and professional cleaning every 2 - 3 years to prevent moisture retention and premature rot.
Individual shakes can split, curl, or deteriorate. Annual inspections catch small problems before they become expensive leaks.
A well-maintained cedar shake roof can last 30 - 40 years, but a neglected one may fail in 15 - 20. Maintenance is not optional with this material.
At $50,000 - $75,000 installed for a 2,500 sq ft roof, cedar shake is a premium investment. Factor in ongoing maintenance costs of $500 - $1,500 per year.

Cedar shake is a beautiful, authentic choice — but only if you're committed to the maintenance. If you love the look but want less upkeep, consider composite shake products or metal shingles designed to mimic cedar's appearance.
What Affects Roofing Cost in Snohomish County
The material cost table above gives you a baseline, but your actual price depends on several factors specific to your home:
Steeper roofs (8/12 pitch and above) require special safety equipment and take longer to install. Expect a 15 - 25% premium for steep-slope work.

Valleys, dormers, skylights, chimneys, and multiple roof planes all add labor time and material waste. A simple gable roof costs significantly less per square foot than a complex hip roof with multiple penetrations.

Until the old roofing comes off, it's impossible to know the full condition of the roof deck. Rot, mold, and water damage are common in Snohomish County homes, especially those with poor ventilation or deferred maintenance.
If the plywood or OSB sheathing underneath is damaged, it must be replaced before new roofing goes on. This adds
depending on how much needs replacing. Partial replacement is common; full replacement is less so but not unusual on older homes.
Tearing off two layers of old shingles costs more in labor and disposal than removing one. Washington allows a maximum of two layers of asphalt shingles.

Homes on hillsides, with limited driveway access, or surrounded by landscaping that needs protection will have higher labor costs. Many homes in the hills around Mukilteo and Lake Stevens face accessibility challenges.

Summer (June through September) is peak roofing season in the PNW. Scheduling in late fall or early spring — when roofers have more availability between rain events — can sometimes mean better pricing and faster scheduling.
A reputable contractor will include a contingency for potential hidden issues, but it's important to understand what might increase your final bill beyond the initial estimate:
Rot and water damage under shingles.
This is the big one. Damaged fascia boards, rafter tails, or decking can add
to your project. Homes built before 1990 or those with a history of deferred maintenance are most at risk. Your contractor should walk you through what they find once the old roof is removed.

Proper attic ventilation is critical for roof longevity in the PNW. If your current ventilation doesn't meet code or isn't adequate for your new roof system, ridge vents, soffit vents, or attic baffles may need to be added. Budget $500 - $2,500.

If your gutters are at the end of their life, it makes sense to replace them during a roof project rather than paying for separate scaffolding and labor later. New gutters run $1,500 - $4,000 for a typical home.

Step flashing, valley flashing, and pipe boot flashing should almost always be replaced during a re-roof. Most contractors include standard flashing in their bid, but custom metalwork around chimneys or complex wall intersections can add $500 - $2,000.

Current building codes may require ice and water shield membrane in valleys and at eaves, improved ventilation ratios, or upgraded underlayment that wasn't required when your roof was last done. These aren't optional — they're code.
Do You Need a Permit to Replace Your Roof in Snohomish County?
This is one of the most misunderstood aspects of roofing in Snohomish County. The rules are actually straightforward once you know them:
Re-roof overlay with the same material type, as long as total layers don't exceed two
Tear-off and replacement with the same material type, as long as roof sheathing is NOT being replaced
Changing roofing material type (e.g., asphalt to metal, or asphalt to cedar shake)
Making any structural changes (adding skylights, modifying roof framing, changing roof pitch)
When a permit is needed, applications can be submitted through
Snohomish County Planning and Development Services (PDS)
. Permit fees typically range from $150 - $500 depending on project scope. Your contractor should handle the permit process for you — if they suggest skipping a required permit, that's a red flag.

For cities within Snohomish County (Everett, Marysville, Lake Stevens, Lynnwood, Mukilteo, etc.), check with the individual city's building department, as some have additional requirements beyond county code.
How Long Does a Roof Replacement Take?
Homeowners are often surprised by how quickly the actual installation goes — and how much time the rest of the process takes:
1 - 3 days of active work for a standard-sized home. Complex roofs or homes requiring extensive deck repair may take 4 - 5 days.
3 - 5 days of active work. Standing seam panels require more precise installation and take longer than shingles.
4 - 7 days. Each shake is hand-placed, making this the most labor-intensive option.

Plan for 2 - 3 weeks from initial consultation to completion. This includes the inspection, estimate, material ordering (some materials have 1 - 2 week lead times), scheduling the crew, and the actual work.
Weather delays are a fact of life in the PNW.

Roofers cannot safely work in rain — the surface is too slippery, and wet conditions compromise adhesive products like roofing cement and ice and water shield. A project scheduled for Monday might not start until Wednesday if rain moves through. Good contractors watch weather windows carefully and will protect any exposed areas with tarps if work needs to pause mid-project. Summer projects have the most predictable timelines; winter and spring projects should build in extra buffer time.
Signs You Need a New Roof
Not sure if it's time? Here are the warning signs Snohomish County homeowners should watch for:
This is the most obvious sign. If you can see bare patches or shingles that have lifted or curled from the ground, your roof's weather protection is compromised.
Asphalt shingles shed granules as they age. A few granules are normal, but heavy accumulation — especially dark, gritty sediment — means the shingles are nearing end of life.
Go into your attic on a sunny day. If you can see pinpoints of light through the roof deck, water is getting in (or will be soon).

If you have asphalt shingles installed 20 or more years ago, it's time for a professional inspection even if nothing looks wrong from the ground. Many issues aren't visible without getting on the roof.
Any visible sagging in the roofline indicates structural problems — possibly compromised decking or rafters. This requires immediate attention.

This is extremely common in Everett's climate. While surface moss can be treated, extensive growth that keeps returning despite treatment suggests moisture is trapped under the shingles, accelerating deterioration.
A failing roof often means failing insulation and ventilation. If your heating costs have crept up without another explanation, poor roof performance could be the culprit.
Brown spots on ceilings or walls, peeling paint, or musty odors in the attic all point to active leaks. Don't wait — water damage compounds quickly.
How much does a new roof cost in Snohomish County?

A new roof in Snohomish County costs $18,000 - $30,000 for architectural asphalt shingles and $40,000 - $60,000 for standing seam metal on an average 2,500 sq ft home. Budget 3-tab asphalt starts around $16,000, while premium materials like cedar shake ($50,000 - $75,000) and tile ($45,000 - $100,000) cost significantly more. Final pricing depends on roof complexity, pitch, hidden damage, and accessibility.
Do I need a permit to replace my roof in Snohomish County?

A re-roof overlay with the same material (2 layers or fewer) or a tear-off and replacement with the same material where sheathing is not replaced does NOT require a permit. A permit IS required when changing material type, replacing roof sheathing, or making structural changes. Apply through mybuildingpermit.com or Snohomish County PDS.
How long does a roof replacement take in the Pacific Northwest?

Asphalt shingle roofs take 1 - 3 days of active work, while metal roofs take 3 - 5 days. The total project timeline is typically 2 - 3 weeks including consultation, material ordering, and scheduling. Weather delays are common in the PNW since roofers cannot work safely in rain.
What is the best roofing material for Washington state rain?

Standing seam metal roofing is the best performer in Washington's rainy climate. It sheds water instantly, resists moss growth, handles heavy rain without degradation, and lasts 50 - 70+ years. Architectural asphalt shingles are the best value option and still perform well with proper ventilation and maintenance.
How often should you replace your roof in the Pacific Northwest?

In the PNW, 3-tab asphalt shingles last 15 - 25 years, architectural shingles last 25 - 40 years, and metal roofs last 40 - 70+ years. The wet climate, moss growth, and temperature swings can shorten lifespan compared to drier regions. Annual inspections help catch problems early and extend your roof's life.

Siding Cost in Everett, WA (2026 Guide)
Published July 2026 by NW General Contractor

For 2026, siding cost Everett homeowners can use for early planning typically ranges from about $7–$18 per square foot installed, while many complete replacements may fall around $18,000–$35,000. Your actual price depends on measured wall area, material, labor, access, finishes, tear-off, and repairs discovered beneath the old siding.
What a siding costs in Everett

There is no single average cost of a siding in Everett that applies to every house. Contractors price exterior wall area, not interior living space, and two homes with similar floor plans can have very different siding quantities. Multiple stories, gables, bump-outs, windows, doors, corners, and attached structures all change the amount of cutting, flashing, trim, staging, and labor required.

For preliminary budgeting, published 2026 Everett estimates suggest installed siding prices typically fall within about $7–$11 per square foot for vinyl, $10–$14 per square foot for engineered wood, and $12–$18 per square foot for fiber cement, depending on product line and scope. Local full-replacement planning ranges commonly extend to approximately $18,000–$35,000 for a house with a typical residential layout. These are planning figures, not a substitute for an on-site estimate. [Everett siding cost benchmark](https://www.redravenexteriors.com/siding/everett)

A siding price per square foot in Everett should be compared only after confirming what it includes. One contractor may include removal, disposal, weather-resistive barrier, flashing, trim, caulking, paint, and cleanup, while another may quote siding installation alone. Ask whether sales tax, permits, equipment, delivery, and allowances for sheathing repairs are included.
Vinyl siding: typically about $7–$11 per square foot installed, depending on scope and product.
Engineered wood siding: typically about $10–$14 per square foot installed, depending on finish and detailing.
Fiber-cement siding: typically about $12–$18 per square foot installed, depending on finish and access.
Complete re-siding: often planned around $18,000–$35,000 for a typical house, with larger or more complex projects potentially outside that range.

Project scope is usually the strongest cost driver. Installing siding over a prepared wall is different from removing several layers, replacing damaged sheathing, correcting flashing, or rebuilding trim around openings. Moisture-related damage cannot always be quantified until removal begins, so a responsible proposal should explain how concealed repairs will be documented and priced.

Materials affect both purchase price and labor. Vinyl panels are comparatively light and quick to handle, while fiber-cement products require different cutting, fastening, clearance, and handling procedures. Engineered wood, cedar, metal, and specialty panels each have their own installation details. Product thickness, profile, exposure, factory color, matching accessories, and manufacturer-required components can change the total.

Finishes matter as well. Primed siding that will be painted on site requires surface preparation, paint, labor, and suitable weather. Factory-finished products may have a higher material price but reduce field painting. Trim width, accent walls, soffits, fascia, corner boards, window surrounds, and transitions between materials should be specified instead of buried in a general finish allowance.

Labor rises when crews need scaffolding, lift access, extensive ladder work, or additional protection for neighboring property and landscaping. Everett homes on tight lots, sloped sites, or busy streets may require more setup and material handling. Permits, inspections, disposal, delivery, and temporary weather protection can also affect the final price.
Measured wall area, stories, gables, corners, windows, doors, and architectural details.
Removal and disposal of existing siding, including the number and type of existing layers.
Condition of sheathing, framing, flashing, weather barrier, and trim after tear-off.
Material profile, finish system, accessory package, and installation requirements.
Crew access, staging, lifts, landscaping protection, cleanup, permits, and inspections.

A targeted repair in the Everett area may typically run about $800–$3,000 when damage is limited and compatible replacement material is available. A larger section or one-wall replacement may commonly fall around $3,000–$8,000. Material-matching difficulties, work above the first story, widespread water damage, or custom trim can move either range higher.

A complete replacement is more likely to fall within approximately $18,000–$35,000 for a typical residential project, depending on measured siding area and material. Larger homes, complicated elevations, premium finishes, extensive sheathing work, or coordinated window and exterior-trim changes may exceed that planning range. A low proposal may also omit items included in a higher proposal, so compare scope before comparing totals.

The installation portion of a full re-side usually takes about 1–3 weeks for an average-size home, depending on crew size, material, architectural complexity, weather, inspections, and concealed repairs. The overall timeline may be longer after including product selection, ordering, scheduling, permit review when applicable, painting, and change-order work. [Everett siding timeline benchmark](https://www.redravenexteriors.com/siding/everett)
Targeted repair: typically about $800–$3,000, depending on access, damage, and material matching.
Partial wall or multi-area repair: commonly about $3,000–$8,000, depending on square footage and underlying conditions.
Typical complete replacement: often around $18,000–$35,000, depending on material, wall area, finishes, and complexity.
Installation timeline for many full re-sides: usually about 1–3 weeks, depending on scope, weather, inspections, and discovered damage.
How to get an accurate estimate

Start with an exterior inspection and field measurements. The estimator should identify siding type, wall dimensions, stories, openings, trim, penetrations, access limitations, and visible signs of moisture trouble. Share any known leaks, past repairs, pest activity, interior staining, or problem walls. Photographs can help with initial screening, but they rarely provide enough information for a dependable final price.

Request a written scope that separates demolition, disposal, wall preparation, siding, trim, flashing, weather barrier, fasteners, sealants, finishes, equipment, cleanup, and applicable permits. If concealed damage cannot be priced in advance, ask for labor and material ranges or a clearly defined change-order method. Confirm how discoveries will be photographed and approved before extra work proceeds.

Do not compare proposals based only on how much does a siding cost at the bottom of the page. Compare measured quantities, product names, profiles, finish specifications, excluded work, allowances, payment schedule, and cleanup responsibilities. Verify that each contractor is properly registered for the work and that the proposal addresses manufacturer installation requirements.

Permit needs depend on the property and work being performed. The City of Everett states that permits are required for most work unless an exemption applies, and its application materials classify exterior alteration as a project type. Confirm the requirement with Everett Permit Services before construction, particularly when the project changes materials, exposes or replaces sheathing, alters structural components, or affects a regulated property. Permit fees vary with project type, size, and valuation. [City of Everett Permit Services](https://www.everettwa.gov/169/Permit-Services)
NW General Contractor serves Everett and Snohomish County. Homeowners can call (425) 286-5639 to arrange a project-specific discussion and estimate.
Ask for field-measured siding area rather than an estimate based only on interior square footage.
Require product, profile, trim, flashing, finish, and weather-barrier details in writing.
Identify exclusions and allowances, especially sheathing, framing, paint, permits, and disposal.
Compare the same scope across proposals and clarify how change orders will be authorized.
Confirm the expected start window and an installation range that accounts for Everett weather.
Smart ways to save without cutting corners

Keep the exterior design focused. Using one primary siding material and a limited accent area generally reduces transitions, specialty trim, ordering complexity, and labor. Standard profiles and readily available colors can also be easier to source than custom products. Ask for alternatives that preserve the needed wall assembly while simplifying purely decorative details.

Repair can be economical when damage is truly isolated and compatible material is obtainable. Replacement may be more practical when failures appear across several walls, the existing product cannot be matched, or repeated repairs would require overlapping setup and finish work. Ask the contractor to price a defined repair option and a broader replacement option so you can compare scope, not assumptions.

Coordinate related exterior work before installation. Planned window, door, electrical, ventilation, or deck-ledger changes can affect siding and flashing. Completing those penetrations in the right sequence may avoid removing new material later. Preserve a contingency range for concealed sheathing or framing repairs instead of spending the entire budget on premium colors or accents.

Savings should not come from omitting flashing, weather management, correct clearances, compatible fasteners, substrate repairs, or manufacturer-required installation details. Those components are less visible than the finish but central to the assembly. A clear proposal and documented preparation provide more value than an unusually low number with major scope gaps.
Simplify material transitions, accent areas, and custom trim where they add little practical value.
Compare factory-finished and field-painted options using complete labor-and-material ranges.
Schedule related window, door, and exterior-penetration work in the correct sequence.
Keep a contingency range for concealed repairs discovered during tear-off.
Choose among complete, comparable scopes instead of selecting solely by the lowest total.
How much does a siding cost in Everett?

For early 2026 planning, siding in Everett typically runs about $7–$18 per square foot installed across common material categories. A complete residential replacement may commonly fall around $18,000–$35,000, depending on measured wall area, material, tear-off, access, finishes, and concealed repairs.
What has the biggest impact on siding cost?

Project scope usually has the largest impact, especially total wall area, removal requirements, building height, architectural complexity, and damage beneath the existing siding. Material and finish selections also matter, but extensive sheathing, framing, flashing, or trim work can change the expected range substantially.
How long does a siding usually take?

Installation for a typical full re-side usually takes about 1–3 weeks, depending on house size, crew size, material, weather, inspections, and underlying damage. The full process may take longer when product ordering, permit review, scheduling, painting, or additional repairs are included.
Do I need a permit for a siding?

A permit may be required depending on the Everett property and scope. Like-for-like minor work may be treated differently from an exterior alteration involving new materials, sheathing, structural repairs, or regulated property conditions. Confirm the applicable requirements with City of Everett Permit Services before work begins.
How do I get an accurate siding estimate?

Arrange an on-site inspection and request a field-measured, itemized proposal. It should define demolition, disposal, wall preparation, siding, trim, flashing, weather barrier, finishes, permits, equipment, cleanup, exclusions, and the method for pricing concealed repairs. NW General Contractor can be reached at (425) 286-5639 for an Everett-area estimate.

Material comparison and pricing guide for homes in Everett and Snohomish County

depending on material, home size, and project complexity. For a typical 1,500-2,000 square foot home, most homeowners land somewhere in the $10,000-$18,000 range.
Why does the range matter so much here? Everett receives

. Add in the persistent gray-sky moisture, wind-driven rain off Puget Sound, and occasional freeze-thaw cycles, and your siding choice directly impacts how well your home handles water intrusion. The wrong material — or the right material installed incorrectly — can lead to rot, mold, and structural damage behind your walls.
This guide breaks down real 2026 pricing for every major siding material, with Pacific Northwest-specific recommendations based on our experience replacing siding across Snohomish County.
Siding Cost by Material (2026 Everett Pricing)
These prices include materials and professional installation for an average-sized home (1,500-2,000 sq ft of siding surface area):

Note: "James Hardie (Premium)" refers to the full James Hardie system with ColorPlus factory-applied finish, HardieWrap weather barrier, and professional certification — a step above standard fiber cement installation.
Best Siding for Pacific Northwest Rain
If there is one thing that separates siding decisions in Everett from those in Phoenix or Dallas, it is moisture. Moisture management is the
for any siding project in the Pacific Northwest, and it should drive every material and installation decision you make.
is the gold standard for PNW homes, and here is why:
— Made from cement, sand, and cellulose fibers, fiber cement does not absorb moisture the way wood does. It will not swell, warp, rot, or become a food source for mold.
— Unlike wood siding that expands and contracts with moisture changes, fiber cement stays put. This means paint lasts longer, joints stay sealed, and water stays outside.
— Fiber cement is non-combustible. While wildfire risk is lower in Everett than eastern Washington, fire resistance adds safety and can reduce insurance premiums.
— Handles wind-blown debris and hail better than vinyl or wood.
Beyond the material itself, how siding is installed matters enormously in the PNW. A

— where a small air gap is created between the siding and the house wrap using furring strips — allows any moisture that penetrates the siding to drain downward and dry out rather than getting trapped against your sheathing. This is especially critical on north-facing walls that receive less sunlight and stay damp longer.
A properly installed rainscreen system includes:
Quality house wrap (like HardieWrap or Tyvek DrainWrap) with sealed seams
Vertical furring strips creating a 3/8" to 3/4" drainage gap
Bottom ventilation to allow airflow behind the siding
Proper flashing around windows, doors, and penetrations

In Everett's climate, we strongly recommend a rainscreen system regardless of which siding material you choose. The incremental cost ($1-$2 per square foot) is minor insurance against the catastrophic cost of moisture damage inside your walls.
Vinyl Siding: Affordable but Know the Risks

Vinyl siding is the cheapest option on the market, and it has legitimate advantages: low material cost, fast installation, no painting required, and decent appearance from the street. For budget-constrained projects, it gets the job done.
However, vinyl has real drawbacks in the Pacific Northwest that you should understand before committing:

— Vinyl panels overlap and interlock but are not sealed. Water gets behind them. If the moisture barrier underneath is inadequate or poorly installed, that water sits against your sheathing and causes rot. This is the single biggest risk with vinyl in Everett.
— Vinyl becomes brittle in freezing temperatures. Everett gets enough cold snaps (especially in January and February) that impact damage from yard debris or even a stiff knock can crack panels.
— Prolonged sun exposure (on south and west-facing walls) causes fading and can warp panels. Dark colors are especially prone to heat warping.
— Strong winds can catch under vinyl panels and pull them loose, especially if installation was rushed or fasteners were over-driven.
If you do go with vinyl, invest in a
underneath and hire an installer who understands PNW moisture management. Cheap vinyl over cheap installation is a recipe for hidden rot that costs far more to fix than the money you saved upfront.
Cedar Siding: Beautiful but High Maintenance

Cedar is the traditional Pacific Northwest siding material. It looks stunning on Craftsman-style homes (which Everett has plenty of), and its natural oils provide inherent resistance to rot and insects. There is a reason cedar has been the go-to choice in the PNW for over a century.
The catch? Maintenance. Lots of it.
— Cedar needs regular treatment to maintain its moisture resistance. Skip a cycle, and the wood starts absorbing water, swelling, and eventually rotting.
— North-facing walls in Everett are a constant battle. Moss grows on cedar in shaded areas, trapping moisture against the wood and accelerating decay. You will need to clean these walls annually.
— Not uncommon in Snohomish County. Cedar is soft enough that woodpeckers and other birds can damage it.

— When you add up staining every 3-5 years ($2,000-$4,000 per cycle for a whole house), cleaning, and spot repairs, cedar often costs more over 20 years than fiber cement that needs almost no maintenance.

Cedar is still a beautiful choice if you genuinely enjoy maintaining your home's exterior and want that authentic PNW aesthetic. Just go in with realistic expectations about the time and money commitment.
Engineered Wood (LP SmartSide): The Middle Ground

LP SmartSide and similar engineered wood products offer an appealing compromise. Made from wood fibers bonded with resins and treated with zinc borate (for rot and termite resistance), engineered wood siding looks remarkably like real wood at a lower cost.
Better moisture resistance than natural wood
— The resin and wax treatment throughout the panel (not just the surface) provides more consistent moisture protection than cedar.
— Deep wood-grain texture that is difficult to distinguish from natural cedar or pine, especially from the street.
— Easier and faster to install, which can reduce labor costs.
— Comes pre-primed and accepts paint well. Holds paint longer than natural wood because it does not expand and contract as much.
— LP SmartSide carries a strong manufacturer warranty when installed per specifications.

The main limitation is that engineered wood is still a wood-based product. While far more resistant than natural wood, it is not as impervious to moisture as fiber cement or metal. Proper installation with adequate flashing and house wrap is essential. For budget-conscious homeowners who want the wood aesthetic without the maintenance burden of cedar, LP SmartSide is a solid choice.
The per-square-foot prices above cover materials and basic installation. But most siding projects include additional work that adds to the total:
$1,000-$3,000 — Depends on how many layers exist and whether there is lead paint (common on pre-1978 homes, which are numerous in Everett).

$1,500-$4,000 — Washington state energy code may require adding insulation when you replace siding. This is especially likely if your home currently has no exterior insulation or the existing insulation is inadequate.
$1,000-$2,000 — Replacing or adding a weather-resistant barrier behind the new siding. Always recommended in the PNW.
$1,000-$3,000 — Window trim, door trim, corner boards, fascia, and soffits often need replacement or updating to match new siding.
$300-$800 — Required for siding replacement in Everett.
on top of your base siding cost to cover these common extras. We always provide a detailed estimate that includes all anticipated costs so there are no surprises.
Do You Need a Permit for Siding Replacement in Everett?

The City of Everett requires a building permit for siding replacement. The good news is that it is a simplified process — no site plan is required for a straightforward re-side, and the turnaround is typically faster than structural permits.
, which serves multiple jurisdictions in Snohomish County.
Key things to know about permits and code:

— When you replace siding, the state energy code may trigger insulation requirements. If your walls do not meet current insulation standards, you may need to add rigid foam insulation or blown-in insulation as part of the project.
— If your home was built before 1978 and has original siding, lead paint abatement rules apply. Your contractor must be EPA Lead-Safe certified.
— Homes near property lines may have fire-resistance requirements that limit material choices.

A licensed contractor handles the permit process as part of the project. This is one of several reasons to avoid unlicensed contractors — they often skip permits, leaving you liable for code violations when you sell your home.
How Long Does Siding Replacement Take?
Timeline depends on material, home size, and weather:
3-5 days — Lightweight panels go up fast with standard tools.
5-10 days — Heavier material requires more labor per panel. Cutting fiber cement is slower than cutting vinyl. Worth the wait.
5-8 days — Similar to fiber cement in installation time, though lighter material.
4-7 days — Custom fabrication may add lead time before installation begins.
for old siding removal and sheathing inspection/repair. If insulation or house wrap needs to be replaced, add another 1-2 days.
Weather delays are real in the PNW.

Siding cannot be installed in heavy rain — paint will not adhere, caulk will not seal, and moisture gets trapped behind panels. Spring and summer are the busiest (and best) seasons for siding work in Everett. Plan ahead and book early — most contractors in Snohomish County are booked 4-8 weeks out during peak season.
Not sure if it is time for new siding? Look for these warning signs:
— Panels that are no longer flat against the wall indicate moisture damage or failed fasteners.
— Probe the bottom edges of siding panels and areas around windows with a screwdriver. If it sinks in easily, the wood is rotting. Bottom courses and areas below windows are the first to go.
Paint that peels within 1-2 years of repainting
— This usually means moisture is migrating through the wall from inside, or the siding itself is failing to hold paint due to deterioration.
Mold or mildew that keeps returning
— Surface cleaning only addresses the symptom. Persistent mold growth means moisture is getting trapped in or behind the siding.
— Failing siding often means failing insulation behind it. If your heating bills have crept up, deteriorated siding and insulation could be the culprit.
— Any opening in your siding is a direct path for water into your wall cavity. In Everett's rain, even small gaps cause big problems over time.
— Brown spots or bubbling paint on interior walls near exterior walls is a serious sign that water is getting through your siding and into the wall structure.
If you are seeing multiple signs on this list, replacement is almost certainly more cost-effective than continued repairs. We offer
throughout Snohomish County — we will tell you honestly whether repair or replacement is the right call.
How much does siding replacement cost in Everett, WA?

Siding replacement in Everett costs $6,000-$28,000 depending on material and home size. Vinyl is the cheapest at $6K-$12K, while premium James Hardie fiber cement runs $22K-$28K for an average-sized home.
What is the best siding material for the Pacific Northwest?

Fiber cement siding (HardiePlank) is the best overall choice for the Pacific Northwest. Its inorganic composition prevents moisture absorption, rot, and warping — critical in a region that gets 37+ inches of rain annually.
Is vinyl siding a good choice for Everett homes?

Vinyl siding is the most affordable option but not ideal for the PNW without excellent installation. It can trap moisture behind panels if improperly installed, leading to rot and mold in the wall cavity. If you go vinyl, invest in a quality moisture barrier and experienced installer.
Do I need a permit for siding replacement in Everett?

Generally yes. The City of Everett requires a building permit for siding replacement. It's a simplified process with no site plan required. Apply through the City of Everett portal or mybuildingpermit.com. Washington energy code may also require insulation upgrades when replacing siding.
How long does siding replacement take?

Vinyl siding takes 3-5 days, fiber cement 5-10 days, and cedar 5-8 days for an average-sized home. Add 1-2 days for old siding removal. Weather delays are common in the PNW since siding cannot be installed in heavy rain.

text_segments: Whole Home Renovation Cost in Everett, WA (2026)
Complete pricing guide for full home remodels in the Everett and Snohomish County area
Published April 2026 | By NW General Contractor

A whole home renovation is one of the biggest investments you can make in your property, and if you're considering one in Everett, Washington, the first thing you need is a realistic understanding of what it costs. In 2026, whole home renovation costs in the Everett area range from
, depending on the scope of work, materials, and current condition of your home.
For a typical 2,000 square foot home, that puts the total investment between

. These numbers are higher than national averages, and there are specific reasons for that. The Puget Sound region has some of the highest labor costs in the country, Washington state's energy code is among the most stringent in the nation, and older homes in Everett frequently come with hidden issues that add to the scope once walls are opened up.

We've been renovating homes throughout Snohomish County for years, and this guide is based on what we actually see in the field. Whether you're updating a 1940s Craftsman in North Everett or doing a full gut remodel on a 1970s rambler near Silver Lake, here's what you can expect to spend.

A cosmetic or partial renovation is a surface-level refresh that updates the look and feel of your entire home without tearing into walls or changing the layout. This is the right approach when the bones of your house are solid but the finishes are dated. For a 2,000 square foot home, expect to spend
Interior walls, ceilings, trim, and doors. A full-home repaint typically runs $8,000-$15,000 depending on square footage and prep work needed.
Luxury vinyl plank, engineered hardwood, or tile throughout the home. Budget $15,000-$35,000 for materials and installation across the full house.
New lighting fixtures, cabinet hardware, door handles, outlet covers, and plumbing fixtures (faucets, showerheads). $5,000-$12,000.
Cabinet refacing in kitchen and baths:
New doors and drawer fronts on existing cabinet boxes, plus new hardware. $8,000-$18,000 for the whole home.
Quartz or granite countertops in the kitchen and bathrooms. $6,000-$15,000.
New vanities, mirrors, tile surrounds, and fixtures without moving plumbing. $8,000-$20,000 per bathroom.
New kitchen appliances and potentially washer/dryer. $5,000-$12,000.

This level works particularly well for older Craftsman and bungalow-style homes in Everett that have good structure and character but need freshening up. You're preserving what works and updating what's worn out. Most cosmetic renovations don't require extensive permitting, though any electrical or plumbing changes will still need permits from the City of Everett.
Full Interior Gut Remodel: $250 - $400 per Square Foot

A gut remodel strips the home down to the studs and rebuilds the interior from scratch. This is the most common approach for homes built in the 1960s through 1980s in the Everett area, many of which have outdated electrical systems, galvanized plumbing, poor insulation, and layouts that don't match how families live today. For a 2,000 square foot home, expect to spend
All interior finishes, insulation, and non-structural elements removed. $15,000-$30,000 in demo and disposal costs.
New 200-amp panel, updated wiring throughout to current code (2021 IRC/NEC), new outlets, switches, and dedicated circuits. $20,000-$40,000.
New supply lines (PEX), drain lines, water heater, and all fixtures. $15,000-$35,000.
Spray foam or high-performance batt insulation to meet Washington's energy code requirements. $10,000-$20,000.
Hanging, taping, mudding, and finishing every wall and ceiling. $15,000-$25,000.
Full kitchen build with semi-custom or custom cabinets, stone countertops, tile backsplash, and quality appliances. $40,000-$75,000.
Fully rebuilt bathrooms with new tile, fixtures, vanities, and waterproofing. $15,000-$40,000 per bathroom.
Everything is new from top to bottom. $20,000-$40,000.
New furnace, ductwork, and potentially air conditioning or a heat pump system to meet current energy codes. $15,000-$30,000.
Gut remodels in Everett often uncover surprises: knob-and-tube wiring, asbestos in floor tiles or insulation, water damage behind walls, and foundation issues. This is why we always recommend a
for homes built before 1980. Those surprises aren't a question of "if" but "what and how much."

A high-end custom renovation goes beyond rebuilding what's there. This level involves architect-designed spaces, structural modifications, and premium materials throughout. It's common in neighborhoods like Mukilteo, Mill Creek, and the waterfront areas of Everett where home values justify the investment. For a 2,000 square foot home, expect to spend
Custom floor plans, 3D renderings, and detailed construction drawings from a licensed architect. $20,000-$50,000.

Removing load-bearing walls, adding beams, opening up floor plans, raising ceilings, and reconfiguring room layouts. Structural engineering adds $5,000-$15,000, and the construction work adds significantly more.
Bump-outs, second-story additions, or expanded footprints that add square footage. $300-$500+ per added square foot.
Built to exact specifications in premium hardwoods with integrated storage solutions, soft-close everything, and custom finishes. $40,000-$80,000.
Natural stone countertops, custom tile work, solid hardwood flooring, designer fixtures, and high-end hardware. Material costs alone can reach $100,000-$200,000+.
Sub-Zero, Wolf, Thermador, or Miele throughout the kitchen. $20,000-$40,000.
Whole-home automation for lighting, HVAC, security, and entertainment. $10,000-$30,000.
Heated floors, steam showers, freestanding tubs, custom vanities, and designer tile. $40,000-$60,000+ per primary bathroom.

At this level, the design phase alone takes 2-4 months before a single hammer swings. Every detail is specified, and the result is a home that looks and feels completely custom-built while retaining the original structure.
When budgeting a whole home renovation, it helps to understand what each room typically costs. Here's what we see across our Snohomish County projects:
Largest single expense; drives home value
Tile, plumbing, and fixtures add up fast
Simpler finishes reduce cost vs. primary

The kitchen and bathrooms together typically account for 40-50% of the total renovation budget. This is where you get the most impact per dollar spent, both for daily livability and resale value. If you need to prioritize, start there.
What Drives Costs in the Everett Area
Whole home renovation costs aren't uniform across the country. Several factors specific to Everett and Snohomish County push prices above the national average:
Labor Demand and the Puget Sound Premium

The Seattle metro area has experienced a sustained construction boom over the past decade, and that demand hasn't let up. Skilled tradespeople in the Puget Sound region command $55-$90 per hour, well above the national average of $40-$60. For a whole home renovation that requires electricians, plumbers, HVAC technicians, carpenters, tile setters, and painters working for months, labor typically represents 35-45% of the total project cost.

Everett's housing stock includes a significant number of homes built between 1900 and 1970. These older homes are full of character but also full of potential issues: knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized steel or even lead plumbing, asbestos in floor tiles and insulation, inadequate foundations, and framing that doesn't meet modern code. Asbestos abatement alone can run $5,000-$15,000 depending on the extent. Every older home should have a 15-20% contingency built into the budget.
A whole home renovation in Everett requires multiple permits, and those fees add up. Depending on the project's scope and valuation, total permit costs typically range from

. This includes building permits, electrical permits, plumbing permits, mechanical permits, and potentially stormwater or environmental review if you're near a critical area or modifying the building envelope.

Washington state has some of the most aggressive energy codes in the country. When you renovate, you're required to bring affected systems up to current code. That means higher-performance insulation, energy-efficient windows, efficient HVAC systems, and LED lighting throughout. These requirements add to the project cost but significantly reduce long-term energy bills and improve comfort.

The Pacific Northwest construction season peaks from April through October, and contractor availability is tightest during summer months. Scheduling your renovation to begin in the late fall or winter months can sometimes yield better availability and pricing, especially for interior-focused work that isn't weather-dependent.
Permits in Everett and Snohomish County
A whole home renovation is a major project from a permitting standpoint. Here's what you need to know:
Required for any structural work, wall modifications, window/door changes, and general construction. This is the master permit that covers the overall scope.
Required for any electrical work, including rewiring, panel upgrades, and new circuits. Must be pulled by a licensed electrician.
Required for any plumbing modifications, new fixtures, or water heater replacement.
Required for HVAC system installation or replacement, ductwork modifications, and exhaust fans.
Within the City of Everett, permits are applied for through the city's online permitting portal. For properties in unincorporated Snohomish County, you can use
, the county's online system. Your general contractor should handle the entire permitting process on your behalf, including preparing the required drawings and documentation.
Plan review for a whole home renovation typically takes

depending on the complexity. Simple interior renovations review faster; projects involving structural changes, additions, or critical area concerns take longer. All work must comply with the 2021 International Residential Code (IRC) as adopted by Washington state, along with the Washington State Energy Code. Inspections are required at multiple stages throughout construction.
Timeline: How Long Does a Whole Home Renovation Take?

One of the most common questions we get is about timeline. A whole home renovation is a significant disruption to your life, and understanding the realistic timeline helps you plan accordingly. Most homeowners move out during a gut remodel or high-end renovation and should plan their living arrangements well in advance.
2-4 months of construction. You may be able to live in the home during portions of the work, though it's uncomfortable.
6-9 months of construction. The home is uninhabitable during this period. Plan for alternative housing.
9-14 months of construction. Complex projects with additions or structural work frequently extend beyond the initial estimate.
1-3 months for the design and planning phase

before construction begins. This includes architectural design (if applicable), material selection, contractor bidding, permit applications, and permit review. Rushing the planning phase to save time almost always leads to change orders and delays during construction, which cost more in the long run.
Is the Design-Build Model Right for You?
For a whole home renovation, the way you structure your project team makes a significant financial difference. There are two common approaches:

You hire an architect to create the design, then separately hire a general contractor to build it. This gives you independent design guidance but creates a handoff between two parties who may not communicate seamlessly. Cost and schedule overruns are more common because the architect's vision doesn't always align with construction realities or budget.

A single firm handles both the design and construction. The designer and builders work together from day one, so the design is created with constructability and budget in mind from the start. There's one contract, one point of contact, and one team responsible for the outcome.
In our experience, the design-build model typically
saves 15-20% compared to the traditional approach

on whole home renovations. The savings come from fewer change orders, better coordination between design intent and construction execution, and elimination of the adversarial dynamic that sometimes develops between architect and contractor. For a project in the $500,000-$800,000 range, that represents $75,000-$160,000 in potential savings.
Tips to Control Costs on a Whole Home Renovation
After renovating homes across Snohomish County, here are our top recommendations for keeping your whole home renovation on budget:

Additions and bump-outs are the fastest way to escalate costs. If your home's square footage works for your needs, invest in improving the existing space rather than expanding it. You'll save on foundation work, roofing, siding, and the extended permit process that comes with additions.

If budget is a constraint, consider phasing the renovation. Do the kitchen, bathrooms, and common areas first (Phase 1), then tackle bedrooms and secondary spaces later (Phase 2). This spreads the financial impact while getting the most impactful rooms done first.

These rooms deliver the highest return on investment and the biggest improvement to daily life. If you have to allocate more budget somewhere and less somewhere else, put the money into the kitchen and primary bathroom.
Budget a 15% contingency for older homes:

If your Everett home was built before 1980, hidden issues are virtually guaranteed. A 15% contingency on a $500,000 project is $75,000 set aside for surprises. If you don't use it all, great. But you won't be forced into cutting corners or stopping work mid-project if problems are found.

Appliances, flooring, and fixtures go on significant sales during Memorial Day, Labor Day, Black Friday, and end-of-year clearance events. If your project timeline allows it, purchasing materials during these windows can save $5,000-$15,000 across a whole home renovation.

Custom everything sounds great but drives costs through the roof and extends timelines. Semi-custom cabinets look nearly as good as full custom at 40-60% of the cost. Standard-size windows are dramatically cheaper than custom sizes. Choose your splurges wisely.
Hire one firm for design and construction:
As discussed above, the design-build model reduces costs, improves communication, and keeps the project on schedule. For a project of this scale, the coordination savings alone justify the approach.
How much does a whole home renovation cost in Everett, WA?

Whole home renovation costs in Everett range from $150 to $450+ per square foot. For a typical 2,000 sq ft home, that translates to $300,000 for a cosmetic refresh up to $900,000 or more for a high-end custom renovation. The final cost depends on scope, materials, and the condition of the existing home. Older homes built before 1980 often run toward the higher end due to hidden issues discovered during construction.
How long does a whole home renovation take in Everett?

A cosmetic renovation typically takes 2-4 months, a full gut remodel runs 6-9 months, and a high-end custom renovation can take 9-14 months. Add 1-3 months on top for the design and planning phase before construction begins. Permit review in Everett and Snohomish County adds 2-6 weeks to the front end of the project.
What permits do I need for a whole home renovation in Everett?

A whole home renovation typically requires building, electrical, plumbing, and mechanical permits. You can apply through the City of Everett's online portal or mybuildingpermit.com for unincorporated Snohomish County. Plan review takes 2-6 weeks depending on the scope. Total permit costs range from $5,000 to $20,000 for a full renovation. Your general contractor should handle the entire permitting process.
Is a design-build contractor better for a whole home renovation?

For most whole home renovations, yes. A design-build firm handles both architectural design and construction under one contract, which typically saves 15-20% compared to hiring a separate architect and general contractor. It also streamlines communication, reduces change orders, and keeps the project on a tighter schedule. For a $500,000+ renovation, that can mean $75,000-$100,000 in savings.
What is the most expensive part of a whole home renovation?

The kitchen is almost always the most expensive room, typically costing $30,000-$75,000 depending on the level of finish. Bathrooms are the second biggest expense at $15,000-$40,000 for the primary bath and $10,000-$25,000 for secondary bathrooms. Together, the kitchen and bathrooms often account for 40-50% of the total renovation budget. Labor is the single largest overall cost category at 35-45% of the total project.

We'll walk through your home, discuss your vision and budget, evaluate the current condition of the structure and systems, and provide a transparent estimate with no hidden costs.
